\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Edge decomposition}
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a class of graphs. The \emph{edge-decomposition problem into $k$ elements of $\mathcal{F}$} asks, for an input graph $G$, whether $E(G)$ can be partitioned into $k$ parts $E_1,\dots,E_k$ so that each spanning subgraph $(V(G),E_i)$ belongs to $\mathcal{F}$. This template subsumes arboricity ($\mathcal{F}$ = forests), thickness ($\mathcal{F}$ = planar graphs), outerthickness ($\mathcal{F}$ = outerplanar graphs) and linear arboricity, among others.

The complexity landscape is starkly bimodal. When $\mathcal{F}$ is the class of forests, the problem is polynomial-time solvable for every $k$: forests are the independent sets of the graphic matroid, so the problem is an instance of matroid union, and it is characterised combinatorially by the Nash-Williams condition
\[
  \text{$G$ decomposes into $k$ forests} \iff |E(H)| \le k\,(|V(H)|-1) \ \text{for every subgraph } H \subseteq G .
\]
For essentially every other natural $\mathcal{F}$ the problem is hard. A recent general theorem states that if $\mathcal{F}$ is closed under topological minors and $1$-sums, has decidable membership, contains a triangle, and is not the class of all graphs, then edge-decomposition into $k \ge 3$ elements of $\mathcal{F}$ is NP-hard --- resolving in particular a long-standing question on outerthickness.

The restriction $k \ge 3$ is not cosmetic. The case $k=2$ remains the frontier, and the natural place to attack it is at the bottom of the hierarchy of admissible classes: the class of triangular forests, for which the two-colour problem has recently been shown to be NP-complete.

\subsection{Contributions}
We develop from first principles the extremal and structural theory underpinning the two-colour problem: a sharp sparsity law (Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp}); sharpness for every odd order (Theorem~\ref{thm:windmill}); an exact threshold for complete graphs (Theorem~\ref{thm:threshold}); a universal clique obstruction (Theorem~\ref{thm:clique}); class properties including $1$-sum closure (Theorem~\ref{thm:onesum}) and decidability (Theorem~\ref{thm:decide}); the certificate reformulation (Theorem~\ref{thm:cert}); and a sharp thickness bound (Theorem~\ref{thm:thick}).

\subsection{Notation}
Graphs are simple and undirected; $n=|V(G)|$, $e=|E(G)|$. A \emph{walk} is a sequence $v_0v_1\cdots v_\ell$ of vertices with consecutive ones adjacent; its \emph{length} is $\ell$. A closed walk is a \emph{cycle} if it is nonempty, its edges are pairwise distinct and its internal vertices are pairwise distinct. $H \le G$ means $H$ is a spanning subgraph of $G$.

\section{Triangular forests}

\begin{definition}\label{def:tf}
A graph $G$ is a \emph{triangular forest} if every cycle of $G$ has length exactly $3$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Block description]\label{prop:blocks}
A graph is a triangular forest if and only if every $2$-connected block of it is a single edge or a triangle.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
If every cycle is a triangle, then no block can have four or more vertices, since a $2$-connected graph on at least four vertices contains a cycle of length at least four; hence every block is an edge or a triangle. Conversely, every cycle lies inside a single block, hence inside a triangle, hence has length $3$.
\end{proof}

Informally, a triangular forest is a forest whose branch structure has been decorated with pairwise edge-disjoint triangles. In particular every acyclic graph is a triangular forest, vacuously.

\begin{proposition}[Closure]\label{prop:closure}
Let $G$ be a triangular forest. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item every spanning subgraph $H \le G$ is a triangular forest;
\item every induced subgraph $G[S]$ is a triangular forest;
\item for every injection $f\colon W \hookrightarrow V(G)$ the pullback $f^*G$ (with $w \sim w'$ iff $f(w) \sim f(w')$) is a triangular forest.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
In each case there is an injective graph homomorphism from the smaller graph into $G$, and the image of a cycle under an injective homomorphism is a cycle of the same length.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Cycle length bound]\label{lem:cyclelen}
If $c$ is a cycle of $G$, then every vertex of $c$ has degree at least $2$, and
$\ell(c) \le |\{x \in V(G) : \deg_G(x) \ge 2\}|$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
A cycle enters and leaves each of its vertices along distinct edges, so those vertices have degree at least $2$; and the $\ell$ internal vertices of $c$ are pairwise distinct.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:threedeg}
If $G$ has at most three vertices of degree at least $2$, then $G$ is a triangular forest.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:membership}
$K_3$ is a triangular forest and $K_4$ is not. Hence the class of triangular forests contains a triangle and is a proper subclass of all graphs.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
$K_3$ has only three vertices, so Corollary~\ref{cor:threedeg} applies (and every cycle in a simple graph has length at least $3$). In $K_4$ the vertices $0,1,2,3$ carry the cycle $0\to1\to2\to3\to0$ of length $4$.
\end{proof}

\section{Degeneracy and the first sparsity bound}

\begin{lemma}[Endpoints of longest paths]\label{lem:endpoint}
Let $G$ be a finite triangular forest and $P = a\,v_1\,v_2\cdots v_m$ a path of maximum length. Then $\deg_G(a) \le 2$, and if $\deg_G(a)=2$ its neighbours are $v_1$ and $v_2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $y \sim a$. If $y \notin V(P)$ then $y\,a\,v_1\cdots v_m$ is a longer path, contradicting maximality. So $y=v_i$; if $i \ge 2$ the edge $av_i$ closes with $a\,v_1\cdots v_i$ a cycle of length $i+1$, which must be $3$, so $i=2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[$2$-degeneracy]\label{thm:degen}
Every finite nonempty triangular forest has a vertex of degree at most $2$; consequently a triangular forest on $n \ge 2$ vertices satisfies $e \le 2n-3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The first claim is Lemma~\ref{lem:endpoint} applied to a maximum-length path. For the bound, induct on $n$: for $n=2$ we have $e \le 1 = 2n-3$; for $n>2$, delete a vertex $v$ with $\deg(v)\le 2$, apply the inductive hypothesis to the triangular forest $G-v$ and add back at most $2$ edges.
\end{proof}

\section{The sharp sparsity law}

\begin{lemma}[The second vertex]\label{lem:second}
Let $G$ be a finite triangular forest, $P=a\,v_1\,v_2\cdots v_m$ a path of maximum length with $m \ge 2$, and suppose $a \sim v_2$. Then $\deg_G(v_1) \le 2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The vertices $a,v_1,v_2$ form a triangle. Let $y \sim v_1$ with $y \notin \{a,v_2\}$. If $y \notin V(P)$, then $y\,v_1\,a\,v_2\,v_3\cdots v_m$ is a path of length $m+1$, contradicting maximality. If $y = v_i$ with $i \ge 4$, then $v_1v_i$ closes with $v_1v_2\cdots v_i$ a cycle of length $i \ge 4$, contradicting Definition~\ref{def:tf}. If $y=v_3$, then $a \to v_1 \to v_3 \to v_2 \to a$ is a cycle of length $4$ on four distinct vertices, again a contradiction. Hence all neighbours of $v_1$ lie in $\{a,v_2\}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Leaf triangle]\label{lem:leaf}
A finite nonempty triangular forest of minimum degree at least $2$ contains an edge $uv$ with $\deg(u)=\deg(v)=2$; moreover $u$ and $v$ have a common neighbour $w$, and $u,v$ have no further neighbours.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Take a maximum-length path $P = a\,v_1\cdots v_m$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:endpoint} and the degree hypothesis, $\deg(a)=2$ with neighbours $v_1, v_2$; by Lemma~\ref{lem:second} and the degree hypothesis, $\deg(v_1)=2$, and its neighbours are $a$ and $v_2$. Take $u=a$, $v=v_1$, $w=v_2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp sparsity law]\label{thm:sharp}
Every triangular forest on $n \ge 1$ vertices satisfies
\[
  2e \le 3(n-1), \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad e \le \left\lfloor \tfrac{3(n-1)}{2}\right\rfloor .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induct on $n$. For $n=1$, $e=0$. Let $n \ge 2$.

\emph{Case A: some vertex $v$ has $\deg(v)\le 1$.} Then $G-v$ is a triangular forest on $n-1$ vertices with at least $e-1$ edges, so $2(e-1)\le 3(n-2)$ and $2e \le 3n-4 \le 3(n-1)$.

\emph{Case B: $\delta(G)\ge 2$.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:leaf} there is a triangle $uvw$ with $\deg(u)=\deg(v)=2$. Deleting $u$ and $v$ removes exactly the three edges $uv,uw,vw$ and exactly two vertices, and leaves a triangular forest on $n-2 \ge 1$ vertices (note $n \ge 3$ here). By induction $2(e-3)\le 3(n-3)$, whence $2e \le 3(n-1)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Budget for a two-part decomposition]\label{cor:budget}
If $G$ on $n \ge 1$ vertices is the edge-disjoint union of two triangular forests, then
$|E(G)| \le 2\lfloor 3(n-1)/2 \rfloor \le 3(n-1)$.
\end{corollary}

\section{Sharpness: the windmill graphs}

\begin{lemma}[Unique far neighbour criterion]\label{lem:far}
Let $x \in V(G)$ and suppose every vertex $y \ne x$ has at most one neighbour other than $x$. Then $G$ is a triangular forest.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $c$ be a cycle. If $x \notin V(c)$, then any vertex of $c$ has two neighbours on $c$, both distinct from $x$, contradicting the hypothesis. So $x \in V(c)$, and rotating $c$ (which preserves length and the cycle property) we may write $c = x \to y_1 \to \cdots \to y_\ell = x$. If $\ell \ge 4$, then $y_2 \ne x$ has the two neighbours $y_1 \ne x$ and $y_3 \ne x$, a contradiction. Hence $\ell=3$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
For $k \ge 0$, the \emph{windmill} (or friendship) graph $F_k$ has vertex set $\{0,1,\dots,2k\}$; the hub $0$ is adjacent to all other vertices, and $2i-1 \sim 2i$ for $1 \le i \le k$. Thus $F_k$ is $k$ triangles glued at the hub.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The bound is attained for every odd order]\label{thm:windmill}
For every $k \ge 0$, the windmill $F_k$ is a triangular forest on $n=2k+1$ vertices with $3k$ edges, so
$2|E(F_k)| = 6k = 3(n-1)$. Hence Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp} is sharp for every odd $n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Every vertex other than the hub has exactly one neighbour besides the hub, so Lemma~\ref{lem:far} applies with $x=0$. The degree sum is $2k + 2\cdot 2k = 6k$, so $|E| = 3k$, and $3(n-1) = 6k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Inspecting the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp}, equality $2e=3(n-1)$ forces every peeling step to be of type~B, i.e.\ to remove a leaf triangle. This suggests that for odd $n$ the maximisers are exactly the connected graphs all of whose blocks are triangles, glued in a tree pattern; the windmills are the star-shaped case.
\end{remark}

\section{The exact threshold for complete graphs}

\begin{definition}
A graph $G$ \emph{decomposes into two triangular forests} if there are triangular forests $G_1,G_2$ on $V(G)$ with $E(G_1)\cap E(G_2)=\emptyset$ and $E(G_1)\cup E(G_2)=E(G)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[$K_5$ decomposes]\label{thm:k5}
The complete graph on $\{0,1,2,3,4\}$ decomposes into the two triangular forests
\[
  G_1 = \{01,\,02,\,12,\,04,\,13\}, \qquad G_2 = \{23,\,24,\,34,\,03,\,14\}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The two sets are disjoint and their union has $10 = \binom{5}{2}$ edges, hence is all of $E(K_5)$. $G_1$ is the triangle $012$ with pendant edges $04$ and $13$; its degree sequence is $(3,3,2,1,1)$, so it has exactly three vertices of degree $\ge 2$ and Corollary~\ref{cor:threedeg} applies. The permutation $(0\,3)(1\,4)$ carries $G_1$ to $G_2$, so the same holds for $G_2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[$K_n$ fails for $n \ge 6$]\label{thm:k6}
For $n \ge 6$, $K_n$ does not decompose into two triangular forests.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $E(K_n)=E(G_1)\sqcup E(G_2)$ with both parts triangular forests, $e_i=|E(G_i)|$. Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp} gives $2e_i \le 3(n-1)$.

If $n \ge 7$: summing, $n(n-1) = 2\binom{n}{2} = 2(e_1+e_2) \le 6(n-1)$, so $n \le 6$, a contradiction.

If $n = 6$: the real-valued count is a dead heat, $n(n-1)=30=6(n-1)$. Use integrality: $2e_i \le 15$ with $e_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ forces $e_i \le 7$, so $e_1+e_2 \le 14 < 15 = \binom{6}{2}$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[How far off is $K_6$?]
An exhaustive scan of all $2^{15}$ edge $2$-colourings of $K_6$ shows that the counting bound of $14$ is not attained: at most $13$ of the $15$ edges can be covered by two triangular forests, a witnessing $7+6$ split being
\[
  G_1=\{03,04,12,13,15,23,34\},\qquad G_2=\{05,14,24,25,35,45\},
\]
which omits the edges $01$ and $02$. Equivalently, $K_6$ minus any single edge is still indecomposable, while $K_6$ minus two disjoint edges is decomposable. This is an enumeration, reported as a computational observation; the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:k6} needs only the bound $14$.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Exact threshold]\label{thm:threshold}
For $n \ge 5$, the complete graph $K_n$ decomposes into two triangular forests if and only if $n=5$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}
Feeding the weaker degeneracy bound $e \le 2n-3$ into the same argument gives only $|E(G)| \le 4n-6$ for decomposable $G$, hence failure of $K_n$ only for $n \ge 8$. The sharp sparsity law is exactly what pushes the threshold from $8$ down to the correct value $6$.
\end{remark}

\section{Monotonicity and the clique obstruction}

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity]\label{thm:mono}
If $G$ decomposes into two triangular forests and $H \le G$, then so does $H$. More generally, if $f\colon W \hookrightarrow V(G)$ is injective and $H \le f^*G$, then $H$ decomposes into two triangular forests.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $E(G)=E(G_1)\sqcup E(G_2)$ with both parts triangular forests, and set $H_i = H \cap f^*G_i$ (taking $f$ the inclusion in the first statement). Each $f^*G_i$ is a triangular forest by Proposition~\ref{prop:closure}(iii), hence so is $H_i$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:closure}(i). Disjointness is inherited edgewise. Finally $f^*G_1 \cup f^*G_2 = f^*(G_1 \cup G_2) = f^*G$, so $H_1 \cup H_2 = H \cap f^*G = H$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Clique obstruction]\label{thm:clique}
If a graph $G$ contains six pairwise adjacent vertices, then $G$ does not decompose into two triangular forests.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The hypothesis provides an injection $f$ with $K_6 \le f^*G$. If $G$ decomposed, Theorem~\ref{thm:mono} would decompose $K_6$, contradicting Theorem~\ref{thm:k6}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Density obstruction]
Corollary~\ref{cor:budget} together with Theorem~\ref{thm:mono} gives a second, quantitative obstruction: if $G$ has a subgraph $H$ on $m$ vertices with $|E(H)| > 3(m-1)$, then $G$ does not decompose. This is the analogue of the Nash-Williams condition --- necessary here, but, unlike in the forest case, not sufficient. That gap is precisely where the computational hardness lives.
\end{remark}

\section{Closure under $1$-sums}

\begin{lemma}[Edges stay on one side]\label{lem:side}
Let $G_1,G_2$ be graphs on a common vertex set such that every vertex incident both to an edge of $G_1$ and to an edge of $G_2$ equals $x$. Let $p=u_0u_1\cdots u_\ell$ be a walk in $G_1\cup G_2$ with $u_i \ne x$ for all $i<\ell$. Then all edges of $p$ lie in $G_1$, or all lie in $G_2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Consecutive edges $u_{i-1}u_i$ and $u_iu_{i+1}$ with $i<\ell$ must lie on the same side: otherwise $u_i$ would be incident to an edge of each, forcing $u_i=x$. Transitivity along the walk finishes the proof.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[$1$-sum closure]\label{thm:onesum}
If $G_1$ and $G_2$ are triangular forests whose supports meet only in the vertex $x$, then $G_1 \cup G_2$ is a triangular forest.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $c$ be a cycle of $G_1 \cup G_2$. If $x$ lies on $c$, rotate $c$ so that it starts and ends at $x$; rotation preserves the cycle property and the length, and the internal vertices of the rotated cycle differ from $x$. Lemma~\ref{lem:side} now applies (in this case, and directly if $x \notin V(c)$), so all edges of $c$ lie in a single $G_i$. Transferring $c$ there, it is a cycle of $G_i$ of the same length, hence a triangle.
\end{proof}

Together with Propositions~\ref{prop:closure} and~\ref{prop:membership} and Theorem~\ref{thm:decide} below, this verifies that triangular forests satisfy all five hypotheses of the general hardness framework, and are minimal among classes doing so.

\section{Certificates, decidability, and NP membership}

\begin{theorem}[Membership is decidable]\label{thm:decide}
For a finite graph $G$ on $n$ vertices, $G$ is a triangular forest if and only if every cycle of length less than $n+1$ has length $3$. In particular membership is decidable by a finite search.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:cyclelen} every cycle has length at most the number of vertices of degree $\ge 2$, hence at most $n < n+1$; so the bounded search sees all cycles.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Efficient test]\label{rem:efficient}
Theorem~\ref{thm:decide} gives decidability, not efficiency. In practice one uses Proposition~\ref{prop:blocks}: compute the block-cut tree in time $O(n+m)$ and accept iff every block has at most three vertices. Equivalently: check that every edge lies in at most one triangle, contract the triangles, and test acyclicity.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Certificate theorem]\label{thm:cert}
A graph $G$ decomposes into two triangular forests if and only if there is an edge $2$-colouring $f\colon E(G) \to \{0,1\}$ such that both colour classes $G_f^0$ and $G_f^1$ are triangular forests.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Leftarrow$) The colour classes are edge-disjoint with union $G$. ($\Rightarrow$) Given $E(G)=E(G_1)\sqcup E(G_2)$, colour an edge $1$ iff it lies in $G_1$. Then $G^1_f = G_1$ by definition, and $G^0_f = G_2$: an edge of $G$ outside $G_1$ lies in $G_2$ by covering, and every edge of $G_2$ lies in $G$ and outside $G_1$ by disjointness.
\end{proof}

The content is structural rather than logical: the witness is a function on the edge set, of size linear in the input. With Remark~\ref{rem:efficient} this places the decision problem in NP; brute-force search over the $2^{|E|}$ colourings shows it is decidable outright. The recent NP-completeness theorem says no essentially better algorithm exists unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$.

\begin{theorem}[Local structure]\label{thm:local}
Let $G$ be a triangular forest. Then $G$ contains no four distinct vertices $a,b,c,d$ with $a\sim b\sim c\sim d\sim a$. Consequently, for every vertex $v$ the neighbourhood of $v$ induces a matching, and every edge lies in at most one triangle.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Such a configuration would be a cycle of length $4$. If $u,w,x$ are neighbours of $v$ with $u \sim w$, $u \sim x$ and $w \ne x$, then $v \to w \to u \to x \to v$ is such a configuration; hence $w=x$. Applying this at an endpoint of an edge $uv$ with two triangles $uvw$, $uvx$ gives $w=x$.
\end{proof}

\section{Triangular thickness}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{triangular thickness} $\ta(G)$ is the least $k$ such that $E(G)$ can be covered by $k$ triangular forests. Since the class is subgraph-closed, covering and partitioning give the same parameter.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp lower bound]\label{thm:thick}
If the edges of $K_n$ ($n \ge 2$) are covered by $k$ triangular forests, then $n \le 3k$; equivalently $\ta(K_n) \ge \lceil n/3 \rceil$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $H_1,\dots,H_k$ be the covering forests with $e_i=|E(H_i)|$. Every edge of $K_n$ lies in some $H_i$, so $\binom{n}{2} \le \sum_i e_i$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp}, $2e_i \le 3(n-1)$, hence $n(n-1) = 2\binom{n}{2} \le 3k(n-1)$. Dividing by $n-1>0$ gives $n \le 3k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Naive bound, for comparison]
Under the same hypotheses, the degeneracy bound $e_i \le 2n-3$ gives only $\binom{n}{2}+3k \le 2kn$, hence $n-1 \le 4k$.
\end{theorem}

Theorem~\ref{thm:thick} improves this by an asymptotic factor $4/3$, and by Theorem~\ref{thm:windmill} its sparsity input is optimal: any further improvement must come from a global obstruction rather than edge counting. That such obstructions exist is shown by $n=6$, where Theorem~\ref{thm:thick} permits $k=2$ but Theorem~\ref{thm:k6} forbids it, so $\ta(K_6) \ge 3$.

\begin{remark}[Conjectured value]
Exploratory randomised search finds covers of $K_n$ by exactly $\lceil n/3 \rceil$ triangular forests for all small $n$ except $n=6$, suggesting $\ta(K_n)=\lceil n/3\rceil$ for $n \ge 3$, $n \ne 6$, and $\ta(K_6)=3$. A cover meeting the counting bound must consist of edge-maximal, pairwise almost edge-disjoint forests --- the structure of a resolvable partial triple system --- and the failure at $n=6$ mirrors the non-existence of a resolvable Steiner triple system of order $6$.
\end{remark}

\section{Algorithms}

\subsection{Membership test}
Compute, for each edge $uv$, the number $|N(u)\cap N(v)|$ of triangles through it; reject if some edge lies in two triangles. Contract the (pairwise edge-disjoint) triangles and accept iff the result is acyclic. Total time $O(m^{3/2})$; the block-cut-tree variant runs in $O(n+m)$.

\subsection{Exhaustive decomposition search with pruning}
Prescreen with the density bound $|E| \le 3(n-1)$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:budget}) and with the $K_6$ test (Theorem~\ref{thm:clique}). Then backtrack over edges, assigning each to the first colour class that remains a triangular forest. Soundness of the partial test follows from subgraph closure: a partial class that is already not a triangular forest can never become one. Worst case $O(2^m \cdot \mathrm{poly})$, but pruning is highly effective in practice.

\subsection{Greedy thickness cover}
Repeatedly extract a maximal triangular forest by scanning the remaining edges in random order and keeping each edge whose addition preserves the class. This Las Vegas procedure finds $\lceil n/3\rceil$-covers of $K_n$ for small $n$ (except $n=6$); every output is verified by the membership test.

\section{Discussion}

The extremal side of the two-colour problem is now complete. Sparsity is settled: $2e \le 3(n-1)$, sharp for every odd $n$, the exact analogue of $e \le n-1$ for forests. The complete-graph threshold is settled: $K_n$ decomposes iff $n \le 5$, with the critical case $n=6$ failing only by integrality --- a one-edge deficit. A universal, locally checkable obstruction is available ($K_6$-freeness), and the decision problem lies in NP with edge $2$-colourings as certificates.

What is not settled --- and, in view of NP-completeness, cannot be settled naively --- is a characterisation of the decomposable graphs. Any conjectured characterisation must be non-local or intractable to check, so the promising directions concern restricted inputs (bounded degree, bounded treewidth, planar) and approximation.

Methodologically, the improvement from $e \le 2n-3$ to $2e \le 3(n-1)$ is not a change of technique but a deepening of one: both proofs peel from the end of a longest path, the sharp one peeling an entire leaf triangle. This recipe should transfer to other classes defined by restricting the palette of admissible blocks.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{conjecture}[Extremal characterisation]
For every $n \ge 1$ there is a triangular forest on $n$ vertices with $\lfloor 3(n-1)/2 \rfloor$ edges; and for odd $n$, equality $2e=3(n-1)$ holds if and only if the graph is connected and every block is a triangle (so there are exactly $(n-1)/2$ blocks, glued in a tree pattern).
\end{conjecture}
The odd case of existence is settled by the windmills; what remains is the even case and the uniqueness half. Equality forces every step of the induction in Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp} to remove a leaf triangle, so the maximisers should be exactly the iterated $1$-sums of triangles --- a class closed under the operation of Theorem~\ref{thm:onesum}.

\begin{conjecture}[Triangular thickness of complete graphs]
$\ta(K_n) = \lceil n/3 \rceil$ for every $n \ge 3$ with $n \ne 6$, and $\ta(K_6)=3$.
\end{conjecture}
The lower bound and the exception are proved; randomised search matches the bound for all $n \le 11$. What remains is a construction for general $n$, which we expect to come from design theory.

\begin{conjecture}[Bounded degree]
For every fixed $\Delta$ there is a finite list of forbidden configurations characterising the graphs of maximum degree at most $\Delta$ that decompose into two triangular forests; consequently the bounded-degree decision problem is polynomial-time solvable.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Large girth]
There is a $g$ such that every graph of girth at least $g$ satisfying $|E(H)| \le 3(|V(H)|-1)$ for all subgraphs $H$ decomposes into two triangular forests.
\end{conjecture}
For girth greater than $3$ a triangular forest is just a forest, so this interpolates towards the Nash-Williams theorem.

\begin{conjecture}[Planar hardness]
Deciding whether a planar graph decomposes into two triangular forests is NP-complete.
\end{conjecture}
Planarity caps the density at $3n-6 \le 3(n-1)$, so the density obstruction never fires and $K_6$ never occurs: the whole difficulty would be structural.

\section*{Summary of results}

Triangular forests: numerical demonstrations of the main results.
=================================================================

A *triangular forest* is a graph in which every cycle has length exactly three;
equivalently, every 2-connected block is a single edge or a triangle.

This self-contained script demonstrates, by explicit computation:

  1. Membership testing for the class (block-based, linear time).
  2. The sharp sparsity law   2e <= 3(n-1)   over all graphs on n <= 7 vertices,

  3. Sharpness: the windmill graphs F_k on n = 2k+1 vertices have 3k edges,
     attaining  2e = 3(n-1).
  4. The exact threshold: K_n decomposes into two triangular forests iff n <= 5,
     with an explicit K_5 certificate and an exhaustive refutation for K_6.
  5. The clique obstruction: any graph containing a K_6 fails to decompose.
  6. Triangular thickness lower bound  n <= 3k  for covers of K_n, and greedy
     covers matching  ceil(n/3)  for small n (n != 6).
  7. Local structure: neighbourhoods induce matchings, so every edge of a
     triangular forest lies in at most one triangle.

Run with:  python3 demo.py
No third-party dependencies.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import random
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Edge = FrozenSet[int]
Graph = Tuple[int, FrozenSet[Edge]]  # (number of vertices, edge set)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basic graph utilities
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def edge(u: int, v: int) -> Edge:
    """The undirected edge {u, v}."""
    if u == v:
        raise ValueError("loops are not allowed in a simple graph")
    return frozenset((u, v))


def make_graph(n: int, pairs: Iterable[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Graph:
    """Build a simple graph on vertices 0..n-1 from a list of pairs."""
    return (n, frozenset(edge(u, v) for u, v in pairs))


def complete_graph(n: int) -> Graph:
    """The complete graph K_n."""
    return make_graph(n, itertools.combinations(range(n), 2))


def windmill(k: int) -> Graph:
    """The windmill (friendship) graph F_k: k triangles glued at the hub 0."""
    pairs: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    for i in range(1, k + 1):
        a, b = 2 * i - 1, 2 * i
        pairs += [(0, a), (0, b), (a, b)]
    return make_graph(2 * k + 1, pairs)


def adjacency(g: Graph) -> Dict[int, Set[int]]:
    """Adjacency lists of a graph."""
    n, edges = g
    adj: Dict[int, Set[int]] = {v: set() for v in range(n)}
    for e in edges:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        adj[u].add(v)
        adj[v].add(u)
    return adj


def degrees(g: Graph) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Degree of every vertex."""
    return {v: len(nbrs) for v, nbrs in adjacency(g).items()}


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Membership test for the class of triangular forests
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def triangles_through(g: Graph, e: Edge) -> List[int]:
    """The vertices completing the edge e to a triangle."""
    adj = adjacency(g)
    u, v = tuple(e)
    return sorted(adj[u] & adj[v])


def is_triangular_forest(g: Graph) -> bool:
    """
    Decide whether every cycle of g has length exactly 3.

    Method (Proposition: block description).  Every edge must lie in at most one
    triangle (otherwise two triangles share an edge and span a 4-cycle).  Then
    contract each triangle to a single vertex and test the result for acyclicity:
    the contracted graph is a forest exactly when every block of g was an edge or
    a triangle.
    """
    n, edges = g
    # (i) every edge lies in at most one triangle
    tri_edges: Set[Edge] = set()
    for e in edges:
        common = triangles_through(g, e)
        if len(common) >= 2:
            return False
        if len(common) == 1:
            tri_edges.add(e)

    # (ii) contract the triangles (union-find over triangle edges)
    parent = list(range(n))

    def find(x: int) -> int:
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
            x = parent[x]
        return x

    def union(x: int, y: int) -> None:
        rx, ry = find(x), find(y)
        if rx != ry:
            parent[rx] = ry

    for e in tri_edges:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        union(u, v)

    # (iii) the quotient must be a forest: count components and remaining edges
    remaining = [e for e in edges if e not in tri_edges]
    quotient_edges: Set[Edge] = set()
    for e in remaining:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        ru, rv = find(u), find(v)
        if ru == rv:
            return False  # a non-triangle edge inside a contracted blob
        q = frozenset((ru, rv))
        if q in quotient_edges:
            return False  # parallel edges in the quotient = a longer cycle
        quotient_edges.add(q)

    roots = {find(v) for v in range(n)}
    # forest test: |E| <= |V| - #components, checked via union-find on the quotient
    parent2 = {r: r for r in roots}

    def find2(x: int) -> int:
        while parent2[x] != x:
            parent2[x] = parent2[parent2[x]]
            x = parent2[x]
        return x

    for q in quotient_edges:
        a, b = tuple(q)
        ra, rb = find2(a), find2(b)
        if ra == rb:
            return False  # cycle in the quotient
        parent2[ra] = rb
    return True


def brute_force_is_triangular_forest(g: Graph) -> bool:
    """Reference implementation: enumerate all cycles and check their lengths."""
    n, edges = g
    adj = adjacency(g)
    for length in range(4, n + 1):
        for verts in itertools.permutations(range(n), length):
            if verts[0] != min(verts):
                continue
            if verts[1] > verts[-1]:
                continue  # kill the reflection
            if all(verts[(i + 1) % length] in adj[verts[i]] for i in range(length)):
                return False
    return True


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2-3. The sharp sparsity law and its extremal graphs
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def max_edges_triangular_forest(n: int) -> Tuple[int, Optional[Graph]]:
    """Exhaustively maximise the edge count over triangular forests on n vertices."""
    all_pairs = list(itertools.combinations(range(n), 2))
    best, witness = 0, None
    for size in range(len(all_pairs), -1, -1):
        found = False
        for subset in itertools.combinations(all_pairs, size):
            g = make_graph(n, subset)
            if is_triangular_forest(g):
                best, witness, found = size, g, True
                break
        if found:
            break
    return best, witness


def sparsity_bound(n: int) -> int:
    """The sharp bound floor(3(n-1)/2) on the number of edges."""
    return (3 * (n - 1)) // 2


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Decomposition into two triangular forests
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def decompose_into_two(g: Graph) -> Optional[Tuple[Graph, Graph]]:
    """
    Search for a partition of E(g) into two triangular forests.

    Backtracking over an edge 2-colouring, using the fact that the class is closed
    under subgraphs: a partial colour class that is already not a triangular forest
    can never become one, so the partial test is a sound pruning rule.
    """
    n, edges = g
    # density prescreen: a decomposable graph satisfies |E| <= 3(n-1)
    if n >= 1 and len(edges) > 3 * (n - 1):
        return None
    order = sorted(edges, key=lambda e: sorted(e))
    part: List[List[Edge]] = [[], []]

    def backtrack(i: int) -> bool:
        if i == len(order):
            return True
        for side in (0, 1):
            part[side].append(order[i])
            if is_triangular_forest((n, frozenset(part[side]))) and backtrack(i + 1):
                return True
            part[side].pop()
        return False

    if not backtrack(0):
        return None
    return (n, frozenset(part[0])), (n, frozenset(part[1]))


def contains_k6(g: Graph) -> bool:
    """Does g contain six mutually adjacent vertices?"""
    n, _ = g
    adj = adjacency(g)
    for six in itertools.combinations(range(n), 6):
        if all(b in adj[a] for a, b in itertools.combinations(six, 2)):
            return True
    return False


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Triangular thickness
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def greedy_cover(g: Graph, tries: int = 4000, seed: int = 20260818) -> List[Graph]:
    """
    Randomised search for a cover of E(g) by few triangular forests.

    Repeatedly peel off a maximal triangular forest under a random edge order and
    keep the best (fewest parts) result over `tries` restarts.  Las Vegas: every
    output part is verified to belong to the class.
    """
    n, edges = g
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    best: Optional[List[Graph]] = None
    for _ in range(tries):
        remaining = set(edges)
        parts: List[Graph] = []
        while remaining:
            order = list(remaining)
            rng.shuffle(order)
            chosen: List[Edge] = []
            for e in order:
                if is_triangular_forest((n, frozenset(chosen + [e]))):
                    chosen.append(e)
            parts.append((n, frozenset(chosen)))
            remaining -= set(chosen)
        if best is None or len(parts) < len(best):
            best = parts
        if best is not None and len(best) <= -(-n // 3):
            break
    assert best is not None
    for p in best:
        assert is_triangular_forest(p)
    return best


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Reporting
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def show(g: Graph) -> str:
    """Readable rendering of a graph's edge set."""
    _, edges = g
    return "{" + ", ".join(f"{min(e)}{max(e)}" for e in sorted(edges, key=lambda e: sorted(e))) + "}"


def banner(text: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print(text)
    print("=" * 78)


def demo_membership() -> None:
    banner("1.  Membership in the class of triangular forests")
    examples: List[Tuple[str, Graph]] = [
        ("K_3  (a triangle)", complete_graph(3)),
        ("K_4", complete_graph(4)),
        ("C_4  (a 4-cycle)", make_graph(4, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 0)])),
        ("path P_5", make_graph(5, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)])),
        ("bowtie F_2", windmill(2)),
        ("two triangles sharing an edge", make_graph(4, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)])),
        ("triangle with two pendant edges", make_graph(5, [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2), (0, 4), (1, 3)])),
    ]
    for name, g in examples:
        fast = is_triangular_forest(g)
        slow = brute_force_is_triangular_forest(g)
        assert fast == slow, f"membership tests disagree on {name}"
        print(f"  {name:34s} n={g[0]}  e={len(g[1]):2d}   triangular forest: {fast}")
    print("\n  (the fast block-based test agrees with brute-force cycle enumeration)")


def demo_sparsity() -> None:
    banner("2-3.  The sharp sparsity law  2e <= 3(n-1)  and its extremal graphs")
    print("   n | max e over all triangular forests | floor(3(n-1)/2) | 2n-3 (weak bound)")
    print("  ---+-----------------------------------+-----------------+------------------")
    for n in range(1, 7):
        best, witness = max_edges_triangular_forest(n)
        assert best == sparsity_bound(n), f"sharp bound violated at n={n}"
        weak = max(2 * n - 3, 0)
        print(f"  {n:2d} | {best:33d} | {sparsity_bound(n):15d} | {weak:17d}")
        if witness is not None and n >= 3:
            print(f"     |   a maximiser: {show(witness)}")
    print("\n  The windmill graphs attain the bound for every odd order:")
    for k in range(1, 7):
        g = windmill(k)
        n, edges = g
        assert is_triangular_forest(g)
        assert 2 * len(edges) == 3 * (n - 1)
        print(f"    F_{k}:  n = {n:2d},  e = {len(edges):2d},  2e = {2*len(edges):2d} = 3(n-1)")


def demo_threshold() -> None:
    banner("4.  The exact threshold:  K_n decomposes into two triangular forests iff n <= 5")
    for n in range(2, 8):
        result = decompose_into_two(complete_graph(n))
        verdict = "YES" if result else "no "
        edges = n * (n - 1) // 2
        budget = 2 * sparsity_bound(n)
        print(f"  K_{n}:  e = {edges:2d},  two-part budget 2*floor(3(n-1)/2) = {budget:2d}   ->  {verdict}")
        if result:
            a, b = result
            print(f"        part 1 = {show(a)}")
            print(f"        part 2 = {show(b)}")
    print()
    print("  The critical case n = 6:  K_6 has 15 edges and the real-valued budget is")
    print("  2 * 3*5/2 = 15 -- a dead heat.  Integrality decides it:  2e <= 15 with e an")
    print("  integer forces e <= 7 per part, so at most 14 < 15 edges can be covered.")
    print("  The decomposition therefore fails by exactly one edge.")


def demo_clique_obstruction() -> None:
    banner("5.  The clique obstruction: a K_6 subgraph forbids decomposition")
    # K_6 plus an isolated vertex and a pendant path: still contains K_6, still fails.
    g = make_graph(9, list(itertools.combinations(range(6), 2)) + [(0, 6), (6, 7), (7, 8)])
    print(f"  Host graph: K_6 with a pendant path attached, n = {g[0]}, e = {len(g[1])}")
    print(f"  contains K_6:                {contains_k6(g)}")
    print(f"  decomposes into two forests: {decompose_into_two(g) is not None}")
    print()
    print("  How much must be removed from K_6 before it decomposes?")
    for removed in ([(4, 5)], [(4, 5), (2, 3)], [(4, 5), (2, 3), (0, 1)]):
        h = make_graph(6, [p for p in itertools.combinations(range(6), 2)
                           if p not in removed])
        res = decompose_into_two(h)
        label = "K_6 minus " + ", ".join(f"{a}{b}" for a, b in removed)
        print(f"    {label:32s} e = {len(h[1]):2d}   decomposes: {res is not None}")
        if res:
            a, b = res
            print(f"        part 1 = {show(a)}")
            print(f"        part 2 = {show(b)}")
    print()
    print("  Deleting a single edge is not enough: the resulting 14 edges exactly")
    print("  saturate the budget 2*floor(3*5/2) = 14, and no split achieves it.")
    print("  Deleting two disjoint edges does suffice.")


def demo_thickness() -> None:
    banner("6.  Triangular thickness of K_n:  the lower bound n <= 3k, and greedy covers")
    print("   n | lower bound ceil(n/3) | greedy cover found | matches?")
    print("  ---+-----------------------+--------------------+---------")
    for n in range(3, 11):
        lb = -(-n // 3)
        cover = greedy_cover(complete_graph(n), tries=2000)
        k = len(cover)
        # verify the cover
        covered: Set[Edge] = set()
        for part in cover:
            assert is_triangular_forest(part)
            covered |= set(part[1])
        assert covered == complete_graph(n)[1]
        assert n <= 3 * k, "the proved lower bound n <= 3k must hold"
        mark = "yes" if k == lb else f"no (needs {k})"
        print(f"  {n:2d} | {lb:21d} | {k:18d} | {mark}")
    print("\n  n = 6 is the exception: counting permits k = 2, but no such cover exists.")


def demo_local_structure() -> None:
    banner("7.  Local structure: neighbourhoods induce matchings")
    for k in range(1, 5):
        g = windmill(k)
        adj = adjacency(g)
        worst = 0

    print("\n  Consequence: in a triangular forest triangles are pairwise edge-disjoint,")
    print("  which is what makes the linear-time membership test correct.")

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import random
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Edge = FrozenSet[int]
Graph = Tuple[int, FrozenSet[Edge]]  # (number of vertices, edge set)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basic graph utilities
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def edge(u: int, v: int) -> Edge:
    """The undirected edge {u, v}."""
    if u == v:
        raise ValueError("loops are not allowed in a simple graph")
    return frozenset((u, v))


def make_graph(n: int, pairs: Iterable[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Graph:
    """Build a simple graph on vertices 0..n-1 from a list of pairs."""
    return (n, frozenset(edge(u, v) for u, v in pairs))


def complete_graph(n: int) -> Graph:
    """The complete graph K_n."""
    return make_graph(n, itertools.combinations(range(n), 2))


def windmill(k: int) -> Graph:
    """The windmill (friendship) graph F_k: k triangles glued at the hub 0."""
    pairs: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    for i in range(1, k + 1):
        a, b = 2 * i - 1, 2 * i
        pairs += [(0, a), (0, b), (a, b)]
    return make_graph(2 * k + 1, pairs)


def adjacency(g: Graph) -> Dict[int, Set[int]]:
    """Adjacency lists of a graph."""
    n, edges = g
    adj: Dict[int, Set[int]] = {v: set() for v in range(n)}
    for e in edges:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        adj[u].add(v)
        adj[v].add(u)
    return adj


def degrees(g: Graph) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Degree of every vertex."""
    return {v: len(nbrs) for v, nbrs in adjacency(g).items()}


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Membership test for the class of triangular forests
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def triangles_through(g: Graph, e: Edge) -> List[int]:
    """The vertices completing the edge e to a triangle."""
    adj = adjacency(g)
    u, v = tuple(e)
    return sorted(adj[u] & adj[v])


def is_triangular_forest(g: Graph) -> bool:
    """
    Decide whether every cycle of g has length exactly 3.

    Method (Proposition: block description).  Every edge must lie in at most one
    triangle (otherwise two triangles share an edge and span a 4-cycle).  Then
    contract each triangle to a single vertex and test the result for acyclicity:
    the contracted graph is a forest exactly when every block of g was an edge or
    a triangle.
    """
    n, edges = g
    # (i) every edge lies in at most one triangle
    tri_edges: Set[Edge] = set()
    for e in edges:
        common = triangles_through(g, e)
        if len(common) >= 2:
            return False
        if len(common) == 1:
            tri_edges.add(e)

    # (ii) contract the triangles (union-find over triangle edges)
    parent = list(range(n))

    def find(x: int) -> int:
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
            x = parent[x]
        return x

    def union(x: int, y: int) -> None:
        rx, ry = find(x), find(y)
        if rx != ry:
            parent[rx] = ry

    for e in tri_edges:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        union(u, v)

    # (iii) the quotient must be a forest: count components and remaining edges
    remaining = [e for e in edges if e not in tri_edges]
    quotient_edges: Set[Edge] = set()
    for e in remaining:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        ru, rv = find(u), find(v)
        if ru == rv:
            return False  # a non-triangle edge inside a contracted blob
        q = frozenset((ru, rv))
        if q in quotient_edges:
            return False  # parallel edges in the quotient = a longer cycle
        quotient_edges.add(q)

    roots = {find(v) for v in range(n)}
    # forest test: |E| <= |V| - #components, checked via union-find on the quotient
    parent2 = {r: r for r in roots}

    def find2(x: int) -> int:
        while parent2[x] != x:
            parent2[x] = parent2[parent2[x]]
            x = parent2[x]
        return x

    for q in quotient_edges:
        a, b = tuple(q)
        ra, rb = find2(a), find2(b)
        if ra == rb:
            return False  # cycle in the quotient
        parent2[ra] = rb
    return True


def brute_force_is_triangular_forest(g: Graph) -> bool:
    """Reference implementation: enumerate all cycles and check their lengths."""
    n, edges = g
    adj = adjacency(g)
    for length in range(4, n + 1):
        for verts in itertools.permutations(range(n), length):
            if verts[0] != min(verts):
                continue
            if verts[1] > verts[-1]:
                continue  # kill the reflection
            if all(verts[(i + 1) % length] in adj[verts[i]] for i in range(length)):
                return False
    return True


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2-3. The sharp sparsity law and its extremal graphs
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def max_edges_triangular_forest(n: int) -> Tuple[int, Optional[Graph]]:
    """Exhaustively maximise the edge count over triangular forests on n vertices."""
    all_pairs = list(itertools.combinations(range(n), 2))
    best, witness = 0, None
    for size in range(len(all_pairs), -1, -1):
        found = False
        for subset in itertools.combinations(all_pairs, size):
            g = make_graph(n, subset)
            if is_triangular_forest(g):
                best, witness, found = size, g, True
                break
        if found:
            break
    return best, witness


def sparsity_bound(n: int) -> int:
    """The sharp bound floor(3(n-1)/2) on the number of edges."""
    return (3 * (n - 1)) // 2


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Decomposition into two triangular forests
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def decompose_into_two(g: Graph) -> Optional[Tuple[Graph, Graph]]:
    """
    Search for a partition of E(g) into two triangular forests.

    Backtracking over an edge 2-colouring, using the fact that the class is closed
    under subgraphs: a partial colour class that is already not a triangular forest
    can never become one, so the partial test is a sound pruning rule.
    """
    n, edges = g
    # density prescreen: a decomposable graph satisfies |E| <= 3(n-1)
    if n >= 1 and len(edges) > 3 * (n - 1):
        return None
    order = sorted(edges, key=lambda e: sorted(e))
    part: List[List[Edge]] = [[], []]

    def backtrack(i: int) -> bool:
        if i == len(order):
            return True
        for side in (0, 1):
            part[side].append(order[i])
            if is_triangular_forest((n, frozenset(part[side]))) and backtrack(i + 1):
                return True
            part[side].pop()
        return False

    if not backtrack(0):
        return None
    return (n, frozenset(part[0])), (n, frozenset(part[1]))


def contains_k6(g: Graph) -> bool:
    """Does g contain six mutually adjacent vertices?"""
    n, _ = g
    adj = adjacency(g)
    for six in itertools.combinations(range(n), 6):
        if all(b in adj[a] for a, b in itertools.combinations(six, 2)):
            return True
    return False


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Triangular thickness
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def greedy_cover(g: Graph, tries: int = 4000, seed: int = 20260818) -> List[Graph]:
    """
    Randomised search for a cover of E(g) by few triangular forests.

    Repeatedly peel off a maximal triangular forest under a random edge order and
    keep the best (fewest parts) result over `tries` restarts.  Las Vegas: every
    output part is verified to belong to the class.
    """
    n, edges = g
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    best: Optional[List[Graph]] = None
    for _ in range(tries):
        remaining = set(edges)
        parts: List[Graph] = []
        while remaining:
            order = list(remaining)
            rng.shuffle(order)
            chosen: List[Edge] = []
            for e in order:
                if is_triangular_forest((n, frozenset(chosen + [e]))):
                    chosen.append(e)
            parts.append((n, frozenset(chosen)))
            remaining -= set(chosen)
        if best is None or len(parts) < len(best):
            best = parts
        if best is not None and len(best) <= -(-n // 3):
            break
    assert best is not None
    for p in best:
        assert is_triangular_forest(p)
    return best


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Reporting
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def show(g: Graph) -> str:
    """Readable rendering of a graph's edge set."""
    _, edges = g
    return "{" + ", ".join(f"{min(e)}{max(e)}" for e in sorted(edges, key=lambda e: sorted(e))) + "}"


def banner(text: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print(text)
    print("=" * 78)


def demo_membership() -> None:
    banner("1.  Membership in the class of triangular forests")
    examples: List[Tuple[str, Graph]] = [
        ("K_3  (a triangle)", complete_graph(3)),
        ("K_4", complete_graph(4)),
        ("C_4  (a 4-cycle)", make_graph(4, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 0)])),
        ("path P_5", make_graph(5, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)])),
        ("bowtie F_2", windmill(2)),
        ("two triangles sharing an edge", make_graph(4, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)])),
        ("triangle with two pendant edges", make_graph(5, [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2), (0, 4), (1, 3)])),
    ]
    for name, g in examples:
        fast = is_triangular_forest(g)
        slow = brute_force_is_triangular_forest(g)
        assert fast == slow, f"membership tests disagree on {name}"
        print(f"  {name:34s} n={g[0]}  e={len(g[1]):2d}   triangular forest: {fast}")
    print("\n  (the fast block-based test agrees with brute-force cycle enumeration)")


def demo_sparsity() -> None:
    banner("2-3.  The sharp sparsity law  2e <= 3(n-1)  and its extremal graphs")
    print("   n | max e over all triangular forests | floor(3(n-1)/2) | 2n-3 (weak bound)")
    print("  ---+-----------------------------------+-----------------+------------------")
    for n in range(1, 7):
        best, witness = max_edges_triangular_forest(n)
        assert best == sparsity_bound(n), f"sharp bound violated at n={n}"
        weak = max(2 * n - 3, 0)
        print(f"  {n:2d} | {best:33d} | {sparsity_bound(n):15d} | {weak:17d}")
        if witness is not None and n >= 3:
            print(f"     |   a maximiser: {show(witness)}")
    print("\n  The windmill graphs attain the bound for every odd order:")
    for k in range(1, 7):
        g = windmill(k)
        n, edges = g
        assert is_triangular_forest(g)
        assert 2 * len(edges) == 3 * (n - 1)
        print(f"    F_{k}:  n = {n:2d},  e = {len(edges):2d},  2e = {2*len(edges):2d} = 3(n-1)")


def demo_threshold() -> None:
    banner("4.  The exact threshold:  K_n decomposes into two triangular forests iff n <= 5")
    for n in range(2, 8):
        result = decompose_into_two(complete_graph(n))
        verdict = "YES" if result else "no "
        edges = n * (n - 1) // 2
        budget = 2 * sparsity_bound(n)
        print(f"  K_{n}:  e = {edges:2d},  two-part budget 2*floor(3(n-1)/2) = {budget:2d}   ->  {verdict}")
        if result:
            a, b = result
            print(f"        part 1 = {show(a)}")
            print(f"        part 2 = {show(b)}")
    print()
    print("  The critical case n = 6:  K_6 has 15 edges and the real-valued budget is")
    print("  2 * 3*5/2 = 15 -- a dead heat.  Integrality decides it:  2e <= 15 with e an")
    print("  integer forces e <= 7 per part, so at most 14 < 15 edges can be covered.")
    print("  The decomposition therefore fails by exactly one edge.")


def demo_clique_obstruction() -> None:
    banner("5.  The clique obstruction: a K_6 subgraph forbids decomposition")
    # K_6 plus an isolated vertex and a pendant path: still contains K_6, still fails.
    g = make_graph(9, list(itertools.combinations(range(6), 2)) + [(0, 6), (6, 7), (7, 8)])
    print(f"  Host graph: K_6 with a pendant path attached, n = {g[0]}, e = {len(g[1])}")
    print(f"  contains K_6:                {contains_k6(g)}")
    print(f"  decomposes into two forests: {decompose_into_two(g) is not None}")
    print()
    print("  How much must be removed from K_6 before it decomposes?")
    for removed in ([(4, 5)], [(4, 5), (2, 3)], [(4, 5), (2, 3), (0, 1)]):
        h = make_graph(6, [p for p in itertools.combinations(range(6), 2)
                           if p not in removed])
        res = decompose_into_two(h)
        label = "K_6 minus " + ", ".join(f"{a}{b}" for a, b in removed)
        print(f"    {label:32s} e = {len(h[1]):2d}   decomposes: {res is not None}")
        if res:
            a, b = res
            print(f"        part 1 = {show(a)}")
            print(f"        part 2 = {show(b)}")
    print()
    print("  Deleting a single edge is not enough: the resulting 14 edges exactly")
    print("  saturate the budget 2*floor(3*5/2) = 14, and no split achieves it.")
    print("  Deleting two disjoint edges does suffice.")


def demo_thickness() -> None:
    banner("6.  Triangular thickness of K_n:  the lower bound n <= 3k, and greedy covers")
    print("   n | lower bound ceil(n/3) | greedy cover found | matches?")
    print("  ---+-----------------------+--------------------+---------")
    for n in range(3, 11):
        lb = -(-n // 3)
        cover = greedy_cover(complete_graph(n), tries=2000)
        k = len(cover)
        # verify the cover
        covered: Set[Edge] = set()
        for part in cover:
            assert is_triangular_forest(part)
            covered |= set(part[1])
        assert covered == complete_graph(n)[1]
        assert n <= 3 * k, "the proved lower bound n <= 3k must hold"
        mark = "yes" if k == lb else f"no (needs {k})"
        print(f"  {n:2d} | {lb:21d} | {k:18d} | {mark}")
    print("\n  n = 6 is the exception: counting permits k = 2, but no such cover exists.")

    for k in range(1, 5):

                if len(partners) > 1:

2*floor(3(n-1)/2) edges.  For K_n that budget first fails at n = 6.

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Edge = FrozenSet[int]


def adjacency(n: int, edges: Iterable[Edge]) -> Dict[int, Set[int]]:
    adj: Dict[int, Set[int]] = {v: set() for v in range(n)}
    for e in edges:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        adj[u].add(v)
        adj[v].add(u)
    return adj


def is_triangular_forest(n: int, edges: Sequence[Edge]) -> bool:
    """Every cycle has length 3: no edge in two triangles, contraction is a forest."""
    adj = adjacency(n, edges)
    tri: Set[Edge] = set()
    for e in edges:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        common = adj[u] & adj[v]
        if len(common) >= 2:
            return False
        if len(common) == 1:
            tri.add(e)
    parent = list(range(n))

    def find(x: int) -> int:
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
            x = parent[x]
        return x

    for e in tri:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        parent[find(u)] = find(v)
    comp = list(range(n))

    def find2(x: int) -> int:
        while comp[x] != x:
            comp[x] = comp[comp[x]]
            x = comp[x]
        return x

    seen: Set[Edge] = set()
    for e in edges:
        if e in tri:
            continue
        u, v = tuple(e)
        ru, rv = find(u), find(v)
        if ru == rv:
            return False
        q = frozenset((ru, rv))
        if q in seen:
            return False
        seen.add(q)
        a, b = find2(ru), find2(rv)
        if a == b:
            return False
        comp[a] = b
    return True


def decompose_into_two(n: int, edges: Sequence[Edge]) -> Optional[Tuple[List[Edge], List[Edge]]]:
    """Backtracking search over edge 2-colourings, pruned by subgraph closure."""
    if len(edges) > 3 * max(n - 1, 0):
        return None
    order = sorted(edges, key=lambda e: sorted(e))
    part: Tuple[List[Edge], List[Edge]] = ([], [])

    def bt(i: int) -> bool:
        if i == len(order):
            return True
        for side in (0, 1):
            part[side].append(order[i])
            if is_triangular_forest(n, part[side]) and bt(i + 1):
                return True
            part[side].pop()
        return False

    return (part[0], part[1]) if bt(0) else None


def deficiency(n: int) -> Tuple[int, Optional[Tuple[List[Edge], List[Edge]]], List[Edge]]:
    """Least number of edges to delete from K_n before the rest splits into two."""
    full = [frozenset(p) for p in itertools.combinations(range(n), 2)]
    for d in range(0, len(full) + 1):
        for omit in itertools.combinations(full, d):
            keep = [e for e in full if e not in omit]
            res = decompose_into_two(n, keep)
            if res is not None:
                return d, res, list(omit)
    return len(full), None, full


def show(edges: Iterable[Edge]) -> str:
    return "{" + ", ".join(f"{min(e)}{max(e)}" for e in sorted(edges, key=lambda e: sorted(e))) + "}"


def main() -> None:
    print(__doc__)
    print("  n |  |E(K_n)| | counting budget | max splittable | deficiency")
    print(" ---+-----------+-----------------+----------------+-----------")
    for n in range(3, 7):
        total = n * (n - 1) // 2
        budget = 2 * ((3 * (n - 1)) // 2)
        d, res, omitted = deficiency(n)
        print(f"  {n} | {total:9d} | {budget:15d} | {total - d:14d} | {d:10d}")
        if res is not None:
            a, b = res
            print(f"    | deleted {show(omitted) if omitted else '(nothing)'}")
            print(f"    | part 1 = {show(a)}")
            print(f"    | part 2 = {show(b)}")
    print()
    print("  Reading the table:  K_3, K_4 and K_5 split with nothing deleted.  For K_6 the")
    print("  counting budget is 14 out of 15 edges, so at least one edge must go -- but in")
    print("  fact two must, and they may be taken disjoint.  The transition is abrupt: a")
    print("  single missing edge is not enough to rescue K_6.")

from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Set, Tuple

class UnionFind:
    """Disjoint-set forest with path halving and union by index."""

    def __init__(self, n: int) -> None:
        self.parent: List[int] = list(range(n))

    def find(self, x: int) -> int:
        while self.parent[x] != x:
            self.parent[x] = self.parent[self.parent[x]]
            x = self.parent[x]
        return x

    def union(self, x: int, y: int) -> bool:
        """Merge the classes of x and y; return False if they were already equal."""
        rx, ry = self.find(x), self.find(y)
        if rx == ry:
            return False
        self.parent[rx] = ry
        return True


def adjacency(n: int, edges: Iterable[Edge]) -> Dict[int, Set[int]]:
    """Adjacency sets of a simple graph on the vertices 0..n-1."""
    adj: Dict[int, Set[int]] = {v: set() for v in range(n)}
    for e in edges:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        adj[u].add(v)
        adj[v].add(u)
    return adj


def is_triangular_forest(n: int, edges: Iterable[Edge]) -> bool:
    """
    Decide whether every cycle of the graph has length exactly three.

    Correctness rests on two facts.  First, in such a graph no edge can lie in two
    triangles: two triangles sharing an edge span a 4-cycle.  Second, once the
    triangles are pairwise edge-disjoint, contracting each of them to a point
    leaves a graph whose cycles correspond exactly to the cycles of length at
    least four of the original; so the contraction must be a forest.

    edges = list(edges)
    adj = adjacency(n, edges)

    triangle_edges: Set[Edge] = set()
    for e in edges:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        common = adj[u] & adj[v]
        if len(common) >= 2:
            return False                       # an edge in two triangles
        if len(common) == 1:
            triangle_edges.add(e)

    blobs = UnionFind(n)
    for e in triangle_edges:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        blobs.union(u, v)

    quotient = UnionFind(n)
    seen: Set[Edge] = set()
    for e in edges:
        if e in triangle_edges:

        ru, rv = blobs.find(u), blobs.find(v)
        if ru == rv:

        q = frozenset((ru, rv))
        if q in seen:
            return False                       # parallel edges: a long cycle
        seen.add(q)
        if not quotient.union(ru, rv):
            return False                       # a cycle in the contraction
    return True

import itertools
from typing import FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Edge = FrozenSet[int]


def sparsity_budget(n: int) -> int:
    """The sharp bound floor(3(n-1)/2) on the edges of a triangular forest of order n."""
    return (3 * max(n - 1, 0)) // 2


def contains_k6(n: int, edges: Iterable[Edge]) -> bool:
    """Does the graph contain six pairwise adjacent vertices?"""
    edge_set = set(edges)
    for six in itertools.combinations(range(n), 6):
        if all(frozenset(p) in edge_set for p in itertools.combinations(six, 2)):
            return True
    return False


def decompose_into_two(
    n: int,
    edges: Sequence[Edge],
    is_triangular_forest,          # callable (n, edges) -> bool
) -> Optional[Tuple[List[Edge], List[Edge]]]:
    """
    Search for a partition of the edge set into two triangular forests.

    Two provably sound prescreens run first:
      * the density test  |E| <= 3(n-1), from the sharp sparsity law applied to
        both parts;
      * the clique test: a K_6 subgraph makes decomposition impossible, because
        decomposability is inherited by subgraphs and K_6 itself fails.

    The search then assigns edges one at a time, testing after each assignment
    that the colour class just extended is still a triangular forest.  This test
    is a *sound* pruning rule because the class is closed under subgraphs: a
    partial class that already contains a long cycle can never be repaired.
    """
    if len(edges) > 3 * max(n - 1, 0):
        return None
    if n >= 6 and contains_k6(n, edges):
        return None

    order: List[Edge] = sorted(edges, key=lambda e: sorted(e))
    part: Tuple[List[Edge], List[Edge]] = ([], [])

    def backtrack(i: int) -> bool:
        if i == len(order):
            return True
        for side in (0, 1):
            if len(part[side]) >= sparsity_budget(n):
                continue                       # this class is already full
            part[side].append(order[i])
            if is_triangular_forest(n, part[side]) and backtrack(i + 1):
                return True
            part[side].pop()
        return False

    return (part[0], part[1]) if backtrack(0) else None

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from typing import Callable, FrozenSet, List, Optional, Sequence, Set

Edge = FrozenSet[int]


def thickness_lower_bound_complete(n: int) -> int:
    """The proved lower bound ceil(n/3) on the triangular thickness of K_n."""
    return -(-n // 3)


def greedy_triangular_cover(
    n: int,
    edges: Sequence[Edge],
    is_triangular_forest: Callable[[int, Sequence[Edge]], bool],
    restarts: int = 2000,
    target: Optional[int] = None,
    seed: int = 0,
) -> List[List[Edge]]:
    """
    Cover the edge set by as few triangular forests as possible.

    Each restart peels maximal triangular forests off the remaining edge set: the
    remaining edges are scanned in a fresh random order and an edge is accepted
    into the current class whenever the class stays inside the graph class.  The
    best (fewest-parts) cover over all restarts is returned, and the search stops
    early if the target number of parts is reached.

    Every part of the returned cover is a triangular forest by construction, so
    the procedure is Las Vegas: the answer is always a valid cover, only the
    number of parts is random.  A single restart runs in
    O(|E| * cost(membership)) time; the sharp sparsity law guarantees that each
    part carries at most floor(3(n-1)/2) edges, so at least
    ceil(|E| / floor(3(n-1)/2)) parts are always needed.
    """
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    best: Optional[List[List[Edge]]] = None

    for _ in range(restarts):
        remaining: Set[Edge] = set(edges)
        parts: List[List[Edge]] = []
        while remaining:
            order = list(remaining)
            rng.shuffle(order)
            chosen: List[Edge] = []
            for e in order:
                if is_triangular_forest(n, chosen + [e]):
                    chosen.append(e)
            parts.append(chosen)
            remaining -= set(chosen)
        if best is None or len(parts) < len(best):
            best = parts
        if target is not None and best is not None and len(best) <= target:
            break

    assert best is not None
    for part in best:
        assert is_triangular_forest(n, part)
    return best

import itertools
import math
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Set, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Edge = FrozenSet[int]
Graph = Tuple[int, FrozenSet[Edge]]


def make_graph(n: int, pairs: Iterable[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Graph:
    return (n, frozenset(frozenset(p) for p in pairs))


def adjacency(g: Graph) -> Dict[int, Set[int]]:
    n, edges = g
    adj: Dict[int, Set[int]] = {v: set() for v in range(n)}
    for e in edges:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        adj[u].add(v)
        adj[v].add(u)
    return adj


def is_triangular_forest(g: Graph) -> bool:
    """Every cycle has length 3: no edge in two triangles, and the contraction is a forest."""
    n, edges = g
    adj = adjacency(g)
    tri_edges: Set[Edge] = set()
    for e in edges:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        common = adj[u] & adj[v]
        if len(common) >= 2:
            return False
        if len(common) == 1:
            tri_edges.add(e)
    parent = list(range(n))

    def find(x: int) -> int:
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
            x = parent[x]
        return x

    for e in tri_edges:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        parent[find(u)] = find(v)
    seen: Set[Edge] = set()
    comp = list(range(n))

    def find2(x: int) -> int:
        while comp[x] != x:
            comp[x] = comp[comp[x]]
            x = comp[x]
        return x

    for e in edges:
        if e in tri_edges:
            continue
        u, v = tuple(e)
        ru, rv = find(u), find(v)
        if ru == rv:
            return False
        q = frozenset((ru, rv))
        if q in seen:
            return False
        seen.add(q)
        a, b = find2(ru), find2(rv)
        if a == b:
            return False
        comp[a] = b
    return True


def max_edges(n: int) -> int:
    """Exact extremal number by exhaustive search (feasible for n <= 7)."""
    pairs = list(itertools.combinations(range(n), 2))
    for size in range(len(pairs), -1, -1):
        for subset in itertools.combinations(pairs, size):
            if is_triangular_forest(make_graph(n, subset)):
                return size
    return 0


def windmill(k: int) -> Graph:
    pairs: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    for i in range(1, k + 1):
        pairs += [(0, 2 * i - 1), (0, 2 * i), (2 * i - 1, 2 * i)]
    return make_graph(2 * k + 1, pairs)


def windmill_positions(k: int) -> Dict[int, Tuple[float, float]]:
    pos: Dict[int, Tuple[float, float]] = {0: (0.0, 0.0)}
    for i in range(1, k + 1):
        base = 2 * math.pi * (i - 1) / k
        for j, off in enumerate((-0.35, 0.35)):
            ang = base + off
            pos[2 * i - 1 + j] = (math.cos(ang), math.sin(ang))
    return pos

    ax.set_xlabel("number of vertices $n$")
    ax.set_ylabel("maximum number of edges")
    ax.set_title("The sparsity frontier of triangular forests")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=9)

    ax2 = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, 2)
    ax2.set_aspect("equal")
    ax2.axis("off")
    ax2.set_title("The extremal family: windmills $F_1,\\dots,F_4$")
    for idx, k in enumerate((1, 2, 3, 4)):

        ax2.text(dx, dy - 1.5, f"$F_{k}$:  $n={2*k+1}$, $e={3*k}$",

    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("sparsity_frontier.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote sparsity_frontier.png")

    main()
