<meta charset="utf-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<title>The Two-Colour Playground</title>
<style>
  :root{
    --bg:#0f1220; --panel:#181c30; --ink:#e9ecf8; --muted:#9aa3c7;
    --red:#ff5d5d; --blue:#5aa9ff; --grey:#4a5178; --ok:#5ce39a; --bad:#ff7a7a;
  }
  *{box-sizing:border-box}
  body{margin:0;background:var(--bg);color:var(--ink);
       font-family:-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,"Segoe UI",Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif}
  .wrap{max-width:1080px;margin:0 auto;padding:26px 20px 46px}
  h1{font-size:1.6rem;margin:0 0 6px;letter-spacing:.2px}
  .sub{color:var(--muted);margin:0 0 22px;line-height:1.55}
  .grid{display:grid;grid-template-columns:minmax(320px,1fr) 340px;gap:22px}
  @media (max-width:860px){.grid{grid-template-columns:1fr}}
  .panel{background:var(--panel);border:1px solid #262c48;border-radius:14px;padding:18px}
  svg{width:100%;height:auto;display:block;touch-action:manipulation}
  .edge{stroke:var(--grey);stroke-width:5;stroke-linecap:round;cursor:pointer;
        transition:stroke .12s ease, stroke-width .12s ease}
  .edge:hover{stroke-width:8}
  .edge.red{stroke:var(--red)}
  .edge.blue{stroke:var(--blue)}
  .vertex{fill:#10142a;stroke:#c8d0f5;stroke-width:2}
  .vlabel{fill:#e9ecf8;font-size:15px;text-anchor:middle;dominant-baseline:central;
          pointer-events:none;font-weight:600}
  .row{display:flex;align-items:center;justify-content:space-between;gap:10px;margin:9px 0}
  .chip{padding:3px 10px;border-radius:999px;font-size:.8rem;font-weight:700}
  .chip.ok{background:rgba(92,227,154,.15);color:var(--ok)}
  .chip.bad{background:rgba(255,122,122,.15);color:var(--bad)}
  .meter{height:9px;border-radius:6px;background:#252b47;overflow:hidden;margin-top:5px}
  .meter > i{display:block;height:100%;border-radius:6px}
  button{background:#242b4c;color:var(--ink);border:1px solid #343c66;border-radius:9px;
         padding:9px 13px;font-size:.88rem;cursor:pointer;margin:4px 4px 0 0}
  button:hover{background:#2d3660}
  button.primary{background:#2f6df0;border-color:#3f7cff}
  button.primary:hover{background:#3b79f7}
  input[type=range]{width:150px}
  .status{margin-top:12px;padding:12px 14px;border-radius:10px;font-size:.92rem;line-height:1.5;
          background:#141a33;border:1px solid #29305a}
  .k{font-family:ui-monospace,SFMono-Regular,Menlo,monospace;color:#cbd4ff}
  .legend{display:flex;gap:16px;color:var(--muted);font-size:.85rem;margin-top:10px;flex-wrap:wrap}
  .swatch{display:inline-block;width:22px;height:5px;border-radius:3px;vertical-align:middle;
          margin-right:6px}
  .hint{color:var(--muted);font-size:.82rem;line-height:1.5;margin-top:12px}
</style>
</head>
<body>
<div class="wrap">
  <h1>The Two-Colour Playground</h1>
  <p class="sub">
    A <b>triangular forest</b> is a graph in which every cycle is a triangle. Colour each edge of the
    complete graph <span class="k">K<sub>n</sub></span> red or blue so that <em>both</em> colour
    classes are triangular forests. Each class may hold at most
    <span class="k">⌊3(n−1)/2⌋</span> edges — watch the budget meters.
    It can be done for <span class="k">n ≤ 5</span>. It is impossible from <span class="k">n = 6</span> on.
  </p>

  <div class="grid">
    <div class="panel">
      <svg id="board" viewBox="0 0 460 460" aria-label="complete graph edge colouring board"></svg>
      <div class="legend">
        <span><span class="swatch" style="background:var(--red)"></span>red class</span>
        <span><span class="swatch" style="background:var(--blue)"></span>blue class</span>
        <span><span class="swatch" style="background:var(--grey)"></span>uncoloured</span>
        <span>click an edge to cycle its colour</span>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="panel">
      <div class="row">
        <label for="nslider"><b>n</b> = <span id="nval">5</span></label>
        <input id="nslider" type="range" min="3" max="7" value="5">
      </div>

      <div class="row"><span>edges of <span class="k">K<sub>n</sub></span></span>
        <span class="k" id="etotal">10</span></div>
      <div class="row"><span>two-part budget</span><span class="k" id="ebudget">12</span></div>

      <hr style="border:0;border-top:1px solid #29305a;margin:14px 0">

      <div class="row"><span style="color:var(--red)"><b>red</b></span>
        <span><span class="k" id="redcount">0</span> / <span class="k" id="cap1">6</span>
          <span class="chip ok" id="redchip">forest ✓</span></span></div>
      <div class="meter"><i id="redmeter" style="width:0%;background:var(--red)"></i></div>

      <div class="row" style="margin-top:14px"><span style="color:var(--blue)"><b>blue</b></span>
        <span><span class="k" id="bluecount">0</span> / <span class="k" id="cap2">6</span>
          <span class="chip ok" id="bluechip">forest ✓</span></span></div>
      <div class="meter"><i id="bluemeter" style="width:0%;background:var(--blue)"></i></div>

      <div class="status" id="status">Colour every edge. Nothing may stay grey.</div>

      <div style="margin-top:12px">
        <button class="primary" id="solve">Auto-solve</button>
        <button id="clear">Clear</button>
        <button id="k5">Show the K₅ certificate</button>
        <button id="k6">Why K₆ fails</button>
      </div>

      <p class="hint">
        <b>The counting argument.</b> A triangular forest on <span class="k">n</span> vertices has at
        most <span class="k">⌊3(n−1)/2⌋</span> edges, so two of them carry at most
        twice that. For <span class="k">K<sub>6</sub></span> the budget is
        <span class="k">7 + 7 = 14</span> but there are <span class="k">15</span> edges — short
        by one. For <span class="k">n ≥ 7</span> the gap only widens.
      </p>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<script>
(function(){
  var n = 5;
  var colour = {};              // "u,v" -> 0 uncoloured, 1 red, 2 blue
  var board  = document.getElementById('board');
  var R = 175, CX = 230, CY = 230;

  function key(u,v){ return Math.min(u,v)+","+Math.max(u,v); }
  function pairs(m){ var out=[]; for(var i=0;i<m;i++) for(var j=i+1;j<m;j++) out.push([i,j]); return out; }
  function pos(v){
    var a = -Math.PI/2 + 2*Math.PI*v/n;
    return [CX + R*Math.cos(a), CY + R*Math.sin(a)];
  }
  function cap(){ return Math.floor(3*(n-1)/2); }

  // --- membership test: every cycle is a triangle ---------------------------
  // No edge in two triangles; contracting the triangles must leave a forest.
  function isTriangularForest(edges){
    var adj = {}, i;
    for(i=0;i<n;i++) adj[i] = {};
    edges.forEach(function(e){ adj[e[0]][e[1]]=1; adj[e[1]][e[0]]=1; });
    var triEdges = {}, ok = true;
    edges.forEach(function(e){
      var common = 0;
      for(var w=0;w<n;w++) if(w!==e[0] && w!==e[1] && adj[e[0]][w] && adj[e[1]][w]) common++;
      if(common >= 2) ok = false;
      if(common === 1) triEdges[key(e[0],e[1])] = 1;
    });
    if(!ok) return false;

    var parent = []; for(i=0;i<n;i++) parent.push(i);
    function find(x){ while(parent[x]!==x){ parent[x]=parent[parent[x]]; x=parent[x]; } return x; }
    edges.forEach(function(e){ if(triEdges[key(e[0],e[1])]) parent[find(e[0])] = find(e[1]); });

    var comp = []; for(i=0;i<n;i++) comp.push(i);
    function find2(x){ while(comp[x]!==x){ comp[x]=comp[comp[x]]; x=comp[x]; } return x; }
    var seen = {};
    for(i=0;i<edges.length;i++){
      var e = edges[i];
      if(triEdges[key(e[0],e[1])]) continue;
      var ru = find(e[0]), rv = find(e[1]);
      if(ru === rv) return false;              // extra edge inside a contracted blob
      var q = key(ru,rv);
      if(seen[q]) return false;                // parallel edges = a long cycle
      seen[q] = 1;
      var a = find2(ru), b = find2(rv);
      if(a === b) return false;                // cycle in the quotient
      comp[a] = b;
    }
    return true;
  }

  function classEdges(c){
    var out = [];
    pairs(n).forEach(function(p){ if(colour[key(p[0],p[1])] === c) out.push(p); });
    return out;
  }

  // --- backtracking solver --------------------------------------------------
  function solve(){
    var all = pairs(n), part = [[],[]], found = false;
    if(all.length > 3*(n-1)) return null;      // density prescreen
    function bt(i){
      if(i === all.length) return true;
      for(var s=0;s<2;s++){
        part[s].push(all[i]);
        if(isTriangularForest(part[s]) && bt(i+1)) return true;
        part[s].pop();
      }
      return false;
    }
    found = bt(0);
    return found ? part : null;
  }

  // --- rendering ------------------------------------------------------------
  function render(){
    while(board.firstChild) board.removeChild(board.firstChild);
    var svgns = "http://www.w3.org/2000/svg";
    pairs(n).forEach(function(p){
      var a = pos(p[0]), b = pos(p[1]);
      var line = document.createElementNS(svgns,"line");
      line.setAttribute("x1",a[0]); line.setAttribute("y1",a[1]);
      line.setAttribute("x2",b[0]); line.setAttribute("y2",b[1]);
      var c = colour[key(p[0],p[1])] || 0;
      line.setAttribute("class","edge" + (c===1?" red":c===2?" blue":""));
      line.addEventListener("click", function(){
        var k = key(p[0],p[1]);
        colour[k] = ((colour[k]||0) + 1) % 3;
        render(); update();
      });
      board.appendChild(line);
    });
    for(var v=0; v<n; v++){
      var q = pos(v);
      var circ = document.createElementNS(svgns,"circle");
      circ.setAttribute("cx",q[0]); circ.setAttribute("cy",q[1]); circ.setAttribute("r",17);
      circ.setAttribute("class","vertex");
      board.appendChild(circ);
      var t = document.createElementNS(svgns,"text");
      t.setAttribute("x",q[0]); t.setAttribute("y",q[1]); t.setAttribute("class","vlabel");
      t.textContent = v;
      board.appendChild(t);
    }
  }

  function update(){
    var red = classEdges(1), blue = classEdges(2);
    var total = n*(n-1)/2, uncoloured = total - red.length - blue.length;
    var rOK = isTriangularForest(red), bOK = isTriangularForest(blue);

    document.getElementById('etotal').textContent  = total;
    document.getElementById('ebudget').textContent = 2*cap();
    document.getElementById('cap1').textContent    = cap();
    document.getElementById('cap2').textContent    = cap();
    document.getElementById('redcount').textContent  = red.length;
    document.getElementById('bluecount').textContent = blue.length;
    document.getElementById('redmeter').style.width  = Math.min(100, 100*red.length/cap())+"%";
    document.getElementById('bluemeter').style.width = Math.min(100, 100*blue.length/cap())+"%";

    var rc = document.getElementById('redchip'), bc = document.getElementById('bluechip');
    rc.textContent = rOK ? "forest ✓" : "long cycle ✗";
    bc.textContent = bOK ? "forest ✓" : "long cycle ✗";
    rc.className = "chip " + (rOK ? "ok" : "bad");
    bc.className = "chip " + (bOK ? "ok" : "bad");

    var s = document.getElementById('status');
    if(!rOK || !bOK){
      s.innerHTML = "A colour class contains a cycle longer than a triangle. Two triangles sharing " +
                    "an edge already span a 4-cycle, so triangles must be pairwise edge-disjoint.";
    } else if(uncoloured > 0){
      s.innerHTML = uncoloured + " edge" + (uncoloured>1?"s":"") + " still grey. " +
        (2*cap() < total
          ? "Careful: the total budget <span class='k'>"+(2*cap())+"</span> is already below the " +
            "<span class='k'>"+total+"</span> edges of K<sub>"+n+"</sub> — this one is hopeless."
          : "Keep going.");
    } else {
      s.innerHTML = "<b style='color:var(--ok)'>Complete decomposition!</b> Every edge is coloured " +
                    "and both classes are triangular forests.";
    }
  }

  function setN(m){
    n = m; colour = {};
    document.getElementById('nval').textContent = n;
    render(); update();
  }

  document.getElementById('nslider').addEventListener('input', function(e){ setN(+e.target.value); });
  document.getElementById('clear').addEventListener('click', function(){ colour = {}; render(); update(); });

  document.getElementById('solve').addEventListener('click', function(){
    var res = solve();
    colour = {};
    if(!res){
      render(); update();
      document.getElementById('status').innerHTML =
        "<b style='color:var(--bad)'>No decomposition exists.</b> Exhaustive search over all edge " +
        "2-colourings of K<sub>"+n+"</sub> came back empty — as the sparsity law predicts for n ≥ 6.";
      return;
    }
    res[0].forEach(function(e){ colour[key(e[0],e[1])] = 1; });
    res[1].forEach(function(e){ colour[key(e[0],e[1])] = 2; });
    render(); update();
  });

  document.getElementById('k5').addEventListener('click', function(){
    setN(5);
    [[0,1],[0,2],[1,2],[0,4],[1,3]].forEach(function(e){ colour[key(e[0],e[1])] = 1; });
    [[2,3],[2,4],[3,4],[0,3],[1,4]].forEach(function(e){ colour[key(e[0],e[1])] = 2; });
    render(); update();
    document.getElementById('status').innerHTML =
      "The classical certificate: <b style='color:var(--red)'>red</b> is the triangle 0-1-2 with " +
      "pendant edges 0-4 and 1-3; <b style='color:var(--blue)'>blue</b> is the triangle 2-3-4 with " +
      "pendant edges 0-3 and 1-4. Each is a triangle with two pendant edges.";
  });

  document.getElementById('k6').addEventListener('click', function(){
    setN(6);
    [[0,3],[0,4],[1,2],[1,3],[1,5],[2,3],[3,4]].forEach(function(e){ colour[key(e[0],e[1])] = 1; });
    [[0,5],[1,4],[2,4],[2,5],[3,5],[4,5]].forEach(function(e){ colour[key(e[0],e[1])] = 2; });
    render(); update();
    document.getElementById('status').innerHTML =
      "K<sub>6</sub> has <span class='k'>15</span> edges. Each class obeys " +
      "<span class='k'>2e ≤ 3·5 = 15</span>, so <span class='k'>e ≤ 7</span>: two classes " +
      "reach at most <span class='k'>14</span>. In fact exhaustive search shows only " +
      "<span class='k'>13</span> edges are reachable — the 7+6 split shown here, with 0-1 and " +
      "0-2 left grey.";
  });

  setN(5);
})();
</script>
</body>
</html>
"
    },
    {
      "title": "Peeling a Triangular Forest: the Sharp Sparsity Law in Action",
      "description": "An animated illustration of the induction that proves 2e <= 3(n-1). The widget generates a random triangular forest by iterated gluing of triangles and pendant edges, lays it out with a small force simulation, and lets the reader peel it apart one step at a time. Each step highlights in orange either a vertex of degree at most one (cost: one vertex, at most one edge) or a leaf triangle -- an edge both of whose endpoints have degree two -- whose deletion costs exactly two vertices and three edges. A running log records the exchange rate of each step while a saturation meter tracks 2e against 3(n-1), so the reader can see why the slope in the bound is 3/2 and which graphs sit at 100 percent. A dedicated button loads the windmill F_4, the extremal graph on nine vertices, which stays saturated all the way down.",
      "html": "<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<title>Peeling a Triangular Forest: the Sharp Sparsity Law in Action</title>
<style>
  :root{--bg:#0f1220;--panel:#181c30;--ink:#e9ecf8;--muted:#9aa3c7;--acc:#5aa9ff;
        --hot:#ff8f5d;--ok:#5ce39a;--line:#5b638f}
  *{box-sizing:border-box}
  body{margin:0;background:var(--bg);color:var(--ink);
       font-family:-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,"Segoe UI",Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif}
  .wrap{max-width:1080px;margin:0 auto;padding:26px 20px 46px}
  h1{font-size:1.5rem;margin:0 0 6px}
  .sub{color:var(--muted);margin:0 0 20px;line-height:1.55}
  .grid{display:grid;grid-template-columns:minmax(320px,1fr) 330px;gap:22px}
  @media (max-width:860px){.grid{grid-template-columns:1fr}}
  .panel{background:var(--panel);border:1px solid #262c48;border-radius:14px;padding:18px}
  svg{width:100%;height:auto;display:block}
  .edge{stroke:var(--line);stroke-width:4;stroke-linecap:round}
  .edge.doomed{stroke:var(--hot);stroke-width:6}
  .vertex{fill:#10142a;stroke:#c8d0f5;stroke-width:2}
  .vertex.doomed{stroke:var(--hot);fill:#3a2015}
  button{background:#242b4c;color:var(--ink);border:1px solid #343c66;border-radius:9px;
         padding:9px 13px;font-size:.88rem;cursor:pointer;margin:4px 4px 0 0}
  button:hover{background:#2d3660}
  button.primary{background:#2f6df0;border-color:#3f7cff}
  .k{font-family:ui-monospace,SFMono-Regular,Menlo,monospace;color:#cbd4ff}
  .row{display:flex;justify-content:space-between;margin:8px 0;font-size:.93rem}
  .bar{height:12px;border-radius:7px;background:#252b47;overflow:hidden;margin:6px 0 14px}
  .bar > i{display:block;height:100%;background:linear-gradient(90deg,#2f6df0,#5ce39a)}

  .log div{margin:3px 0;color:var(--muted)}
  .log b{color:var(--ink)}

<body>
<div class="wrap">
  <h1>Peeling a Triangular Forest</h1>
  <p class="sub">
    The sharp sparsity law <span class="k">2e ≤ 3(n−1)</span> is proved by repeatedly
    stripping the graph down. If some vertex has degree at most 1, delete it: that costs
    <span class="k">1</span> vertex and at most <span class="k">1</span> edge. Otherwise a longest-path
    argument produces a <b>leaf triangle</b> — an edge both of whose endpoints have degree two
    — and deleting those two vertices costs exactly <span class="k">2</span> vertices and
    <span class="k">3</span> edges. That exchange rate <span class="k">3 : 2</span> is
    precisely the slope in the bound. Press <b>Peel</b> and watch it happen.
  </p>

  <div class="grid">
    <div class="panel">
      <svg id="canvas" viewBox="0 0 500 420"></svg>
    </div>
    <div class="panel">
      <div class="row"><span>vertices <span class="k">n</span></span><span class="k" id="nv">–</span></div>
      <div class="row"><span>edges <span class="k">e</span></span><span class="k" id="ev">–</span></div>
      <div class="row"><span><span class="k">2e</span></span><span class="k" id="lhs">–</span></div>
      <div class="row"><span><span class="k">3(n−1)</span></span><span class="k" id="rhs">–</span></div>
      <div class="bar"><i id="fill" style="width:0%"></i></div>
      <div class="row"><span>saturation</span><span class="k" id="sat">–</span></div>

      <div style="margin-top:10px">
        <button class="primary" id="peel">Peel one step</button>
        <button id="auto">Peel to the end</button>
        <button id="fresh">New random forest</button>
        <button id="wind">Windmill F₄</button>
      </div>

      <div class="log" id="log"></div>

      <p class="hint">
        A graph at <span class="k">100%</span> saturation is <b>extremal</b>: every peeling step must
        be a leaf triangle, so every block is a triangle. The windmill <span class="k">F<sub>k</sub></span>
        — <span class="k">k</span> triangles sharing a hub — is the standard example, with
        <span class="k">n = 2k+1</span> and <span class="k">e = 3k</span>.
      </p>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<script>
(function(){
  var V = [], E = [], pos = {}, log = document.getElementById('log');
  var svg = document.getElementById('canvas'), svgns = "http://www.w3.org/2000/svg";

  function deg(v){ var d=0; E.forEach(function(e){ if(e[0]===v||e[1]===v) d++; }); return d; }
  function nbrs(v){
    var out=[]; E.forEach(function(e){ if(e[0]===v) out.push(e[1]); else if(e[1]===v) out.push(e[0]); });
    return out;
  }

  // ---- random triangular forest: iterated pendant edges and glued triangles ----
  function randomForest(){
    V = [0]; E = []; var next = 1;
    var steps = 7 + Math.floor(Math.random()*3);
    for(var s=0;s<steps;s++){
      var anchor = V[Math.floor(Math.random()*V.length)];
      if(Math.random() < 0.62){                       // glue a triangle at `anchor`
        var a = next++, b = next++;
        V.push(a,b); E.push([anchor,a],[anchor,b],[a,b]);
      } else {                                        // hang a pendant edge
        var c = next++;
        V.push(c); E.push([anchor,c]);
      }
    }
    layout(); redraw(); resetLog("A random triangular forest: triangles and bridges glued in a tree pattern.");
  }

  function windmill(k){
    V = [0]; E = [];
    for(var i=1;i<=k;i++){ var a=2*i-1, b=2*i; V.push(a,b); E.push([0,a],[0,b],[a,b]); }
    layout(); redraw(); resetLog("The windmill F" + k + ": " + k + " triangles at a common hub. It sits exactly on the bound.");
  }

  // ---- crude force layout ----
  function layout(){
    pos = {};
    V.forEach(function(v,i){
      var a = 2*Math.PI*i/V.length;
      pos[v] = [250 + 130*Math.cos(a) + (Math.random()-0.5)*20,
                210 + 130*Math.sin(a) + (Math.random()-0.5)*20];
    });
    for(var it=0; it<420; it++){
      var fx = {}, fy = {};
      V.forEach(function(v){ fx[v]=0; fy[v]=0; });
      V.forEach(function(u){ V.forEach(function(v){
        if(u===v) return;
        var dx = pos[u][0]-pos[v][0], dy = pos[u][1]-pos[v][1];
        var d2 = Math.max(40, dx*dx+dy*dy);
        fx[u] += 5200*dx/d2; fy[u] += 5200*dy/d2;
      });});
      E.forEach(function(e){
        var dx = pos[e[1]][0]-pos[e[0]][0], dy = pos[e[1]][1]-pos[e[0]][1];
        var d = Math.max(1, Math.hypot(dx,dy)), f = 0.035*(d-78);
        fx[e[0]] += f*dx/d; fy[e[0]] += f*dy/d;
        fx[e[1]] -= f*dx/d; fy[e[1]] -= f*dy/d;
      });

### A guided tour of triangular forests, sparsity laws, and the edge that breaks everything

---

## 1. The game

Take a graph. Colour every edge red or blue. The rule: **each colour class, on its own, must be a
graph in which every cycle is a triangle.** Such a graph is called a *triangular forest* — picture
a tree whose branch points have been thickened into little triangles.

That is the whole problem. It sounds like a puzzle, and for small graphs it is one. Try it: below
is the complete graph $K_n$ with every pair of vertices joined. Click an edge to make it red, click
again for blue, again to clear it. The panel keeps score.

Start at $n=5$ and try to colour all ten edges. Then push the slider to $n=6$ and try again. Then
press **Auto-solve** and see what an exhaustive search says.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

> **What you should have discovered.** $K_5$ can be done — in fact there is a beautiful symmetric
> solution. $K_6$ cannot, no matter how you try. Everything below is the story of *why*, and of
> exactly where the boundary sits.

<details>
<summary><b>Why "every cycle is a triangle" is the same as "every block is an edge or a triangle"</b></summary>

A *block* (or 2-connected component) is a maximal piece of the graph that stays connected when you
delete any single vertex. Every cycle lives inside a single block. A 2-connected graph on four or
more vertices always contains a cycle of length at least four. So if every cycle is a triangle, no
block can have four or more vertices, and each is therefore a single edge or a single triangle.
Conversely, if every block is an edge or a triangle then every cycle lies inside a triangle and has
length three.

This is why the picture "a forest with triangular knots" is exactly right.
</details>

---

## 2. Why one extra cycle length changes everything

Decomposing a graph into $k$ *forests* — no cycles at all — is a solved, polynomial-time problem.
Forests are the independent sets of a matroid, and the classical
[Nash-Williams theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arboricity) says a graph splits into $k$
forests exactly when every subgraph $H$ satisfies $|E(H)| \le k(|V(H)|-1)$. Edmonds' matroid-union
algorithm turns that criterion into an efficient procedure.

Triangular forests are one notch more permissive: cycles are allowed, but only the shortest kind.
And they form **no matroid**. Whether you may add an edge depends on *where* it sits, not just on
what you already have. The moment matroid theory stops applying, greedy strategies fail and the
search space branches exponentially. Deciding whether a graph splits into two triangular forests is
NP-complete — the two-colour case is genuinely hard, while the forest case is easy.

Everything we can still prove is *extremal*: counting arguments that pin down exactly how many
edges fit, and what happens at the boundary.

---

## 3. The first structural fact: triangles are lonely

Here is the observation everything else grows from.

> **Matching Neighbourhood Theorem.** In a triangular forest, the neighbours of any vertex induce a
> matching. Equivalently, **every edge lies in at most one triangle**.

The proof is one line. If a vertex $v$ had neighbours $u, w, x$ with $u \sim w$ and $u \sim x$ and
$w \ne x$, then
$$v \to w \to u \to x \to v$$
would be a cycle of length four on four distinct vertices. Forbidden. So two triangles never share
an edge: they may touch at a vertex, never along a side.

That immediately rules out $K_4$: its vertices $0,1,2,3$ carry the four-cycle
$0 \to 1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 0$. So triangular forests contain a triangle but are not all graphs — they
are a genuine, proper, minimal class.

---

## 4. The sparsity law, and the algorithm that proves it

How many edges can a triangular forest on $n$ vertices have? A tree has $n-1$. A triangular forest
can do better, but not much better.

> **Sharp Sparsity Law.** A triangular forest on $n$ vertices has at most
> $\left\lfloor \tfrac{3(n-1)}{2} \right\rfloor$ edges; equivalently $2e \le 3(n-1)$.

The proof is an algorithm: peel the graph down to nothing, and count what each peeling step costs.

- If some vertex has degree at most $1$, delete it: **1 vertex, at most 1 edge**.
- Otherwise, a longest-path argument hands you a **leaf triangle** — an edge both of whose endpoints
  have degree exactly two. Deleting those two vertices removes **2 vertices and exactly 3 edges**.

The second exchange rate, $3$ edges per $2$ vertices, is the binding one. That is where the slope
$3/2$ comes from. Watch it run:

{{interactive_demo:1}}

<details>
<summary><b>The longest-path argument in full</b></summary>

Let $P = a \, v_1 \, v_2 \cdots v_m$ be a path of maximum length.

*Step 1: $a$ has degree at most two.* Every neighbour of $a$ must lie on $P$ (otherwise extend $P$
and contradict maximality). A neighbour $v_i$ with $i \ge 2$ closes a cycle of length $i+1$, which
must equal $3$, so $i = 2$. Hence the neighbours of $a$ are among $\{v_1, v_2\}$.

*Step 2: if $a$ also has $v_2$ as a neighbour, then $v_1$ has degree at most two too.* Suppose $y$
is a neighbour of $v_1$ other than $a$ and $v_2$.
 - If $y$ is off the path, then $y \, v_1 \, a \, v_2 \, v_3 \cdots v_m$ is a *longer* path —
   contradiction. (Notice the trick: we reroute through the triangle $a v_1 v_2$, gaining a vertex.)
 - If $y = v_i$ with $i \ge 4$, the edge $v_1 v_i$ closes a cycle of length $i \ge 4$ —
   contradiction.
 - If $y = v_3$, then $a \to v_1 \to v_3 \to v_2 \to a$ is a four-cycle — contradiction.

So in a triangular forest of minimum degree at least two, the edge $a v_1$ has both endpoints of
degree two: a leaf triangle. Deleting $a$ and $v_1$ removes exactly the three edges
$a v_1, a v_2, v_1 v_2$. Induction on $n$ now gives $2e \le 3(n-1)$.
</details>

Is $3/2$ really the truth, or just what this proof yields? It is the truth, and the witnesses are
the **windmills** $F_k$: $k$ triangles all sharing one hub vertex, on $n = 2k+1$ vertices with
exactly $3k$ edges, so $2e = 6k = 3(n-1)$ exactly. Press **Windmill $F_4$** in the widget above and
watch the saturation meter read $100\%$ all the way down.

<details>
<summary><b>Why a windmill is a triangular forest — without checking a single cycle</b></summary>

There is a slick criterion. Suppose some vertex $x$ is distinguished, and *every other vertex has at
most one neighbour besides $x$*. Then every cycle is a triangle.

Why: a cycle avoiding $x$ would give each of its vertices two neighbours other than $x$ —
impossible. So $x$ lies on the cycle, and we may rotate the cycle to start and end at $x$:
$x \to y_1 \to y_2 \to \cdots \to x$. If the cycle had length four or more, then $y_2$ would have
the two neighbours $y_1 \ne x$ and $y_3 \ne x$ — impossible again. So the length is three.

In a windmill, every non-hub vertex has exactly one neighbour besides the hub: its partner in its
triangle. Done.
</details>

## 5. The threshold: where two colours run out

Now combine the two halves. If a graph on $n$ vertices splits into two triangular forests, then
$$|E| \le 2\left\lfloor \tfrac{3(n-1)}{2}\right\rfloor \le 3(n-1).$$

For $K_n$, which has $\binom{n}{2} = \tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$ edges, that demands
$\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2} \le 3(n-1)$, i.e. $n \le 6$. So $n \ge 7$ dies by pure counting.

And $n = 6$? Here the real-valued count is a **dead heat**: $K_6$ has $15$ edges and the budget is
$3\cdot 5 = 15$. Integrality decides it. Each part obeys $2e \le 15$, and $e$ is a whole number, so
$e \le 7$. Two parts reach $14$. One edge short.

> **Complete-Graph Threshold Theorem.** For $n \ge 5$, the complete graph $K_n$ decomposes into two
> triangular forests if and only if $n = 5$.

The $K_5$ certificate is worth savouring: **red** is the triangle $0$–$1$–$2$ with pendant edges
$0$–$4$ and $1$–$3$; **blue** is the triangle $2$–$3$–$4$ with pendant edges $0$–$3$ and $1$–$4$.
Two identical shapes, rotated into each other, tiling all ten edges. Press
*Show the $K_5$ certificate* in the first widget to see it.

{{visualization:1}}

How abrupt is the transition really? Exhaustively:

{{demo:1}}

The answer is stark. Deleting a *single* edge from $K_6$ is not enough — the resulting $14$-edge
graph exactly saturates the counting budget and still fails. You must delete **two** edges, and two
disjoint ones suffice.

---

## 6. A certificate of impossibility you can carry around

The threshold theorem is about complete graphs, but it upgrades instantly, because the property is
inherited downwards: if $G$ splits as $G_1 \sqcup G_2$ and $H$ is a subgraph of $G$, then
$H \cap G_1$ and $H \cap G_2$ split $H$, and each is a subgraph of a triangular forest, hence a
triangular forest.

> **Clique Obstruction Theorem.** If a graph contains six mutually adjacent vertices, it does not
> decompose into two triangular forests.

This is the two-colour analogue of "an odd cycle forbids a proper $2$-colouring of the vertices": a
small, local, checkable certificate of failure. Because the general problem is NP-complete, no
finite list of such obstructions can capture everything — but this one is free, and it is the first
thing any algorithm should look for.

{{algorithm:1}}

---

## 7. Recognising the class efficiently

Everything above needs one primitive: *is this graph a triangular forest?* The definition quantifies
over all cycles, which sounds expensive. It is not, thanks to §3.

{{algorithm:0}}

The idea: check that no edge lies in two triangles (§3 says a triangular forest must pass this),
then contract every triangle to a single point and test the result for acyclicity. Once triangles are
pairwise edge-disjoint, the cycles of the contraction are exactly the original cycles of length four
or more — so the contraction is a forest precisely when every original cycle was a triangle.

This also settles a soft but important point: the decision problem lies in **NP**. A witness is just
a red/blue labelling of the edges — an object of size linear in the input — and verifying it means
running the recogniser twice.

<details>
<summary><b>The formal statement of the certificate theorem</b></summary>

A graph $G$ decomposes into two triangular forests **if and only if** there is a function
$f : E(G) \to \{\text{red}, \text{blue}\}$ such that both preimages are triangular forests.

The forward direction takes $f$ to be the indicator of membership in the first part; the reverse is
immediate since the two colour classes are edge-disjoint with union $G$. The content is not logical
but structural: an existential quantifier over abstract pairs of graphs becomes an existential
quantifier over labellings, which is what "certificate" means.
</details>

---

## 8. Beyond two colours: triangular thickness

If two triangular forests cannot cover $K_n$, how many can? Call the minimum the *triangular
thickness* $\theta_\triangle(K_n)$. Feed the sharp sparsity law into the same counting:
each part carries at most $\tfrac{3(n-1)}{2}$ edges, and $K_n$ has $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$, so

$$k \ge \frac{n}{3}, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \theta_\triangle(K_n) \ge \left\lceil \frac{n}{3} \right\rceil.$$

The weaker degeneracy bound $e \le 2n-3$ would give only $n - 1 \le 4k$; the sharp law improves this
by an asymptotic factor $4/3$. And since the sparsity input is provably optimal, **no further
improvement can come from counting** — any better bound needs a global obstruction, exactly like the
integrality argument at $n = 6$.

Is $\lceil n/3 \rceil$ the truth? Randomised search says yes for every small $n$ except the familiar
troublemaker:

{{algorithm:2}}

<details>
<summary><b>The lone exception at $n = 6$, and a design-theoretic echo</b></summary>

For $n = 6$ counting permits $k = 2$, but the integrality argument forbids it, so
$\theta_\triangle(K_6) \ge 3$. This is the *only* place in the explored range where the counting
bound is not achieved.

There is a suggestive parallel. A cover meeting the counting bound must consist of forests that are
simultaneously edge-maximal (windmill-like) and pairwise almost edge-disjoint — the structure of a
[resolvable triple system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steiner_system). Resolvable Steiner triple
systems exist for orders $\equiv 3 \pmod 6$, and the smallest failure of the naive count in that
theory is likewise at order $6$. We expect the general construction to come from design theory
rather than from ad hoc graph gluing.
</details>

---

## 9. The full computational tour

Everything asserted above, computed from scratch and checked against the theorems: membership
testing (fast versus brute force), the exact extremal numbers for $n \le 6$, the windmill family, the
threshold, the clique obstruction, the thickness covers, and the local structure.

{{demo:0}}

---

## 10. Where the story goes next

The extremal side is complete: sparsity is settled and sharp; the complete-graph threshold is exact;
a local obstruction is available; the problem is in NP. What is missing — and, given NP-completeness,
must be missing in any naive form — is a *characterisation* of the decomposable graphs.

The open questions that look most tractable:

1. **Extremal uniqueness.** For odd $n$, are the graphs with $2e = 3(n-1)$ exactly the connected
   graphs all of whose blocks are triangles? Equality forces every peeling step to remove a leaf
   triangle, so this should be an equality analysis of the existing induction.
2. **Exact thickness.** Is $\theta_\triangle(K_n) = \lceil n/3\rceil$ for all $n \ne 6$? The lower
   bound is proved; only a construction is missing.
3. **Bounded degree.** Is there, for each fixed maximum degree, a finite list of forbidden
   configurations — making the bounded-degree problem polynomial?
4. **Large girth.** Is the density condition $|E(H)| \le 3(|V(H)|-1)$ *sufficient* once the girth is
   large? This interpolates towards Nash-Williams.
5. **Planar hardness.** Planarity caps the density below the obstruction threshold and forbids
   $K_6$ outright. Is the problem still NP-complete there — i.e. is the hardness structural rather
   than a density phenomenon?

Two colours. One extra cycle length. An entire complexity class of difference.

section Criterion

/-- Rotating a closed walk preserves its length. -/
theorem length_rotate [DecidableEq V] {v x : V} (c : G.Walk v v) (h : x ∈ c.support) :

def FanAdj (a b : ℕ) : Prop :=

open SimpleGraph Finset

variable {V : Type*}

/-- `G` **decomposes into two triangular forests** when its edges can be split into two
edge-disjoint triangular forests. -/
def DecomposesIntoTwo (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ G₁ G₂ : SimpleGraph V, IsTriangularForest G₁ ∧ IsTriangularForest G₂ ∧
    Disjoint G₁ G₂ ∧ G₁ ⊔ G₂ = G

section Counting

variable [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]

/-- The edges of a graph covered by two graphs are covered by their edges. -/
theorem card_edgeFinset_le_of_le_sup {G G₁ G₂ : SimpleGraph V} [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    [DecidableRel G₁.Adj] [DecidableRel G₂.Adj] (h : G ≤ G₁ ⊔ G₂) :
    #G.edgeFinset ≤ #G₁.edgeFinset + #G₂.edgeFinset := by
  classical
  have hsub : G.edgeFinset ⊆ G₁.edgeFinset ∪ G₂.edgeFinset := by
    intro e he
    induction e with
    | _ x y =>
      simp only [mem_edgeFinset, mem_edgeSet] at he
      rcases h he with hh | hh <;> simp [hh]
  exact le_trans (card_le_card hsub) (card_union_le _ _)

into two triangular forests has at most `4n - 6` edges. -/
theorem card_edgeFinset_add_six_le_of_decomposesIntoTwo (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]

  have hb₂ := card_edgeFinset_add_three_le G₂ h₂ hcard
  have hle : #G.edgeFinset ≤ #G₁.edgeFinset + #G₂.edgeFinset :=

  omega

    intro a b hab

    rw [hcs]

/-!
# The sharp sparsity bound for triangular forests

A connected triangular forest on `n` vertices with `t` triangular blocks has `n - 1 + t` edges
and `2t ≤ n - 1`, so `2e ≤ 3(n-1)`.  Here we prove this sharp bound
(`TriangularForest.two_mul_card_edgeFinset_le`) without developing block decompositions, by
refining the longest-path argument of `Logic.TriangularForest.Sparsity`:

* `TriangularForest.degree_second_le_two` — if `p = a → v₁ → v₂ → ⋯` is a longest path in a
  triangular forest and `a` is also adjacent to `v₂` (which happens as soon as `a` has degree
  two), then the *second* vertex `v₁` also has degree at most two.  Neighbours of `v₁` off the
  path would allow the reroute `y → v₁ → a → v₂ → ⋯`, which is longer; neighbours further along
  the path close a cycle of length `≥ 4`, except for the vertex `v₃`, which is excluded by the
  4-cycle `a → v₁ → v₃ → v₂ → a`.
* `TriangularForest.exists_adj_degree_le_two` — hence a triangular forest of minimum degree at
  least two contains an *edge* both of whose endpoints have degree two (a leaf triangle).
* Deleting such a pair removes two vertices and exactly three edges, which powers the induction
  giving `2e ≤ 3(n-1)`.

As a consequence `Kₙ` fails to decompose into two triangular forests already for `n ≥ 6`, which
combined with `TriangularForest.completeGraph_decomposesIntoTwo_five` pins the threshold
exactly: `Kₙ` decomposes into two triangular forests if and only if `n ≤ 5`.
-/

namespace TriangularForest

open SimpleGraph Finset

variable {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V}

/-- A walk of length at least two starts with two `cons`. -/
theorem exists_cons_cons_of_two_le_length {a b : V} (p : G.Walk a b) (h : 2 ≤ p.length) :
    ∃ (v₁ v₂ : V) (h₀₁ : G.Adj a v₁) (h₁₂ : G.Adj v₁ v₂) (r : G.Walk v₂ b),
      p = Walk.cons h₀₁ (Walk.cons h₁₂ r) := by
  cases p with
  | nil => simp at h
  | cons h₀₁ q =>
    cases q with
    | nil => simp at h
    | cons h₁₂ r => exact ⟨_, _, h₀₁, h₁₂, r, rfl⟩

variable [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableRel G.Adj]

/-- **The second vertex of a longest path.**  In a triangular forest, if `a → v₁ → v₂ → ⋯` is a

theorem degree_second_le_two (hG : IsTriangularForest G)

    have e2 : a ≠ v₂ := ha₂.ne
    have e3 : a ≠ y := fun h => hya h.symm
    have e4 : v₁ ≠ v₂ := h₁₂.ne

      have hnew : (Walk.cons hadj.symm (Walk.cons h₀₁.symm (Walk.cons ha₂ r))).IsPath := by
        rw [Walk.cons_isPath_iff, Walk.cons_isPath_iff, Walk.cons_isPath_iff]
        refine ⟨⟨⟨hr, har'⟩, ?_⟩, ?_⟩
        · simp only [Walk.support_cons, List.mem_cons, not_or]

    set q := r.takeUntil y hys with hq

      have hrlen : 0 < r.length := by
        have hle := r.length_takeUntil_le hys
        rw [← hq] at hle
        omega
      have hy1 : r.getVert 1 = y := by
        have := r.getVert_support_idxOf hys
        rwa [← r.length_takeUntil hys, ← hq, hlen1] at this
      have hv₂y : G.Adj v₂ y := by
        have := r.adj_getVert_succ (i := 0) hrlen
        simpa [hy1] using this
      have hcyc : (Walk.cons h₀₁ (Walk.cons hadj (Walk.cons hv₂y.symm
          (Walk.cons ha₂.symm Walk.nil)))).IsCycle := by
        rw [Walk.cons_isCycle_iff]
        refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
        · simp [Walk.isPath_def, e4, e5, e1.symm, e2.symm, e3.symm, e6.symm]
        · simp [e1, e2, e3, e4, e5, e1.symm]
      have hcl := hG _ hcyc
      simp only [Walk.length_cons, Walk.length_nil] at hcl
      omega
    · -- `y` is further along: it closes a cycle of length `q.length + 2 ≥ 4`.
      have hedge : s(y, v₁) ∉ (Walk.cons h₁₂ q).edges := by
        simp only [Walk.edges_cons, List.mem_cons, Sym2.eq_iff, not_or]
        refine ⟨by simp [e4, e5.symm, e6.symm], ?_⟩
        intro hmem
        exact hqv₁ (Walk.snd_mem_support_of_mem_edges q hmem)
      have hcyc : (Walk.cons hadj.symm (Walk.cons h₁₂ q)).IsCycle := by
        rw [Walk.cons_isCycle_iff]
        refine ⟨?_, hedge⟩
        rw [Walk.cons_isPath_iff]
        exact ⟨hqp, hqv₁⟩
      have hcl := hG _ hcyc
      simp only [Walk.length_cons] at hcl
      omega
  calc G.degree v₁ = #(G.neighborFinset v₁) := (card_neighborFinset_eq_degree G v₁).symm
    _ ≤ #({a, v₂} : Finset V) := Finset.card_le_card hsub
    _ ≤ 2 := Finset.card_insert_le _ _ |>.trans (by simp)

/-- **Leaf triangle lemma.**  A finite triangular forest with minimum degree at least two
contains an edge whose two endpoints both have degree at most two. -/
theorem exists_adj_degree_le_two [Nonempty V] (hG : IsTriangularForest G)
    (hmin : ∀ v : V, 2 ≤ G.degree v) :
    ∃ u v : V, G.Adj u v ∧ G.degree u ≤ 2 ∧ G.degree v ≤ 2 := by
  classical
  obtain ⟨a, b, p, hp, hmax⟩ := exists_maxPath G

  -- position `2` along `p` is occupied by a neighbour of `a`
  have himg : (G.neighborFinset a).image (fun x => p.support.idxOf x) = {1, 2} := by
    refine Finset.eq_of_subset_of_card_le ?_ ?_
    · intro i hi
      simp only [Finset.mem_image] at hi
      obtain ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩ := hi
      have := maxPath_neighbor_idx hG p hp hmax hx
      simpa using this
    · rw [Finset.card_image_of_injOn (maxPath_idx_injOn p hp hmax)]
      simp [card_neighborFinset_eq_degree, hdega']
  have h2img : (2 : ℕ) ∈ (G.neighborFinset a).image (fun x => p.support.idxOf x) := by
    rw [himg]; simp
  simp only [Finset.mem_image] at h2img
  obtain ⟨x, hx, hx2⟩ := h2img
  have hxs : x ∈ p.support := maxPath_neighbor_mem_support p hp hmax hx
  have hxgv : p.getVert 2 = x := by
    have := p.getVert_support_idxOf hxs
    rwa [hx2] at this
  have hlen : 2 ≤ p.length := by
    by_contra hcon
    push_neg at hcon
    have hidx : p.support.idxOf x < p.support.length := List.idxOf_lt_length_of_mem hxs
    rw [Walk.length_support] at hidx
    omega
  obtain ⟨v₁, v₂, h₀₁, h₁₂, r, rfl⟩ := exists_cons_cons_of_two_le_length p hlen
  have ha₂ : G.Adj a v₂ := by
    have : v₂ = x := by simpa using hxgv
    rw [this]
    exact (G.mem_neighborFinset a x).1 hx
  refine ⟨a, v₁, h₀₁, hdega, degree_second_le_two hG h₀₁ h₁₂ r hp hmax ha₂⟩

end Leaf

section Counting

/-- Deleting a vertex `u` drops the degree of each of its neighbours by at least one. -/
theorem degree_induce_compl_singleton_add_one_le [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    [DecidableRel G.Adj] {u v : V} (h : G.Adj v u) (hv : v ∈ ({u}ᶜ : Set V)) :
    (G.induce ({u}ᶜ : Set V)).degree ⟨v, hv⟩ + 1 ≤ G.degree v := by
  classical
  have hmaps : Set.MapsTo (fun w : ({u}ᶜ : Set V) => (w : V))
      (((G.induce ({u}ᶜ : Set V)).neighborFinset ⟨v, hv⟩ : Finset _) : Set _)
      (((G.neighborFinset v).erase u : Finset V) : Set V) := by
    intro w hw
    simp only [Finset.mem_coe, mem_neighborFinset] at hw
    simp only [Finset.mem_coe, Finset.mem_erase, mem_neighborFinset]
    refine ⟨fun hh => ?_, hw⟩
    exact (w.2 : (w : V) ∈ ({u}ᶜ : Set V)) (by simp [hh])
  have hcard := Finset.card_le_card_of_injOn _ hmaps (Subtype.val_injective.injOn)
  rw [Finset.card_erase_of_mem (by simpa using h)] at hcard
  have hpos : 1 ≤ G.degree v := by
    rw [← card_neighborFinset_eq_degree]
    exact Finset.card_pos.2 ⟨u, by simpa using h⟩
  rw [card_neighborFinset_eq_degree, card_neighborFinset_eq_degree] at hcard
  omega

private theorem sharp_aux : ∀ n : ℕ, ∀ (V : Type u) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj], Fintype.card V = n → 1 ≤ n →
    IsTriangularForest G → 2 * #G.edgeFinset ≤ 3 * (n - 1) := by
  intro n
  induction n using Nat.strong_induction_on with
  | _ n ih =>
    intro V _ _ G _ hcard hn hG
    rcases eq_or_lt_of_le hn with h1 | h2
    · -- a single vertex carries no edge
      have hch := G.card_edgeFinset_le_card_choose_two
      rw [hcard, ← h1] at hch
      rw [show Nat.choose 1 2 = 0 from rfl] at hch
      omega
    · have hne : Nonempty V := Fintype.card_pos_iff.1 (by omega)
      by_cases hmin : ∀ v : V, 2 ≤ G.degree v
      · -- minimum degree two: delete a leaf triangle, i.e. two adjacent degree-two vertices
        obtain ⟨u, v, huv, hu, hv⟩ := exists_adj_degree_le_two hG hmin
        have hn3 : 3 ≤ n := by
          have hlt : G.degree u < Fintype.card V := G.degree_lt_card_verts u
          have := hmin u
          omega
        have hvs : v ∈ ({u}ᶜ : Set V) := by simpa using huv.ne'
        have hG'tf : IsTriangularForest (G.induce ({u}ᶜ : Set V)) := hG.induce _
        have hcard' : Fintype.card ({u}ᶜ : Set V) = n - 1 := by
          rw [Fintype.card_compl_set]
          simp [hcard]
        have hedges' : #(G.induce ({u}ᶜ : Set V)).edgeFinset = #G.edgeFinset - G.degree u := by
          rw [G.card_edgeFinset_induce_compl_singleton u, G.card_edgeFinset_deleteIncidenceSet u]
        have hdegu : G.degree u ≤ #G.edgeFinset := G.degree_le_card_edgeFinset u
        -- now delete `v` inside the smaller graph
        have hdegv' : (G.induce ({u}ᶜ : Set V)).degree ⟨v, hvs⟩ + 1 ≤ G.degree v :=
          degree_induce_compl_singleton_add_one_le huv.symm hvs
        have hG''tf : IsTriangularForest
            ((G.induce ({u}ᶜ : Set V)).induce ({(⟨v, hvs⟩ : ({u}ᶜ : Set V))}ᶜ)) :=
          hG'tf.induce _
        have hcard'' : Fintype.card ({(⟨v, hvs⟩ : ({u}ᶜ : Set V))}ᶜ : Set ({u}ᶜ : Set V))
            = n - 2 := by
          rw [Fintype.card_compl_set]
          simp only [Set.card_singleton, hcard']
          omega
        have hedges'' : #((G.induce ({u}ᶜ : Set V)).induce
              ({(⟨v, hvs⟩ : ({u}ᶜ : Set V))}ᶜ)).edgeFinset
            = #(G.induce ({u}ᶜ : Set V)).edgeFinset
              - (G.induce ({u}ᶜ : Set V)).degree ⟨v, hvs⟩ := by
          rw [(G.induce ({u}ᶜ : Set V)).card_edgeFinset_induce_compl_singleton ⟨v, hvs⟩,
            (G.induce ({u}ᶜ : Set V)).card_edgeFinset_deleteIncidenceSet ⟨v, hvs⟩]
        have hdegv'' : (G.induce ({u}ᶜ : Set V)).degree ⟨v, hvs⟩
            ≤ #(G.induce ({u}ᶜ : Set V)).edgeFinset :=
          (G.induce ({u}ᶜ : Set V)).degree_le_card_edgeFinset ⟨v, hvs⟩
        have hIH := ih (n - 2) (by omega)
          ({(⟨v, hvs⟩ : ({u}ᶜ : Set V))}ᶜ : Set ({u}ᶜ : Set V))
          ((G.induce ({u}ᶜ : Set V)).induce ({(⟨v, hvs⟩ : ({u}ᶜ : Set V))}ᶜ)) hcard''
          (by omega) hG''tf
        omega
      · -- some vertex has degree at most one: delete it
        push_neg at hmin
        obtain ⟨v, hv⟩ := hmin
        have hcard' : Fintype.card ({v}ᶜ : Set V) = n - 1 := by
          rw [Fintype.card_compl_set]
          simp [hcard]
        have hedges' : #(G.induce ({v}ᶜ : Set V)).edgeFinset = #G.edgeFinset - G.degree v := by
          rw [G.card_edgeFinset_induce_compl_singleton v, G.card_edgeFinset_deleteIncidenceSet v]
        have hdegv : G.degree v ≤ #G.edgeFinset := G.degree_le_card_edgeFinset v
        have hIH := ih (n - 1) (by omega) ({v}ᶜ : Set V) (G.induce ({v}ᶜ : Set V)) hcard'
          (by omega) (hG.induce _)
        omega

/-- **Sharp sparsity bound.**  A triangular forest on `n ≥ 1` vertices satisfies
`2e ≤ 3(n - 1)`; equality holds exactly for connected unions of triangles glued in a tree
pattern. -/
theorem two_mul_card_edgeFinset_le {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V)
    [DecidableRel G.Adj] (hG : IsTriangularForest G) (hcard : 1 ≤ Fintype.card V) :
    2 * #G.edgeFinset ≤ 3 * (Fintype.card V - 1) :=
  sharp_aux (Fintype.card V) V G rfl hcard hG

end Counting

/-- A graph on `n ≥ 1` vertices decomposing into two triangular forests has at most
`2⌊3(n-1)/2⌋` edges. -/
theorem card_edgeFinset_le_of_decomposesIntoTwo' {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (hG : DecomposesIntoTwo G)
    (hcard : 1 ≤ Fintype.card V) :
    ∃ e₁ e₂ : ℕ, #G.edgeFinset ≤ e₁ + e₂ ∧ 2 * e₁ ≤ 3 * (Fintype.card V - 1) ∧
      2 * e₂ ≤ 3 * (Fintype.card V - 1) := by
  classical
  obtain ⟨G₁, G₂, h₁, h₂, -, hsup⟩ := hG
  refine ⟨#G₁.edgeFinset, #G₂.edgeFinset, ?_, two_mul_card_edgeFinset_le G₁ h₁ hcard,
    two_mul_card_edgeFinset_le G₂ h₂ hcard⟩

# Triangular forests

A *triangular forest* is a graph in which every 2-connected block is a single edge or a
triangle.  Equivalently (and this is the definition we use, since it is the most convenient
one to reason with) a graph is a triangular forest exactly when **every cycle has length 3**.

cycle of length at least four, and two triangles sharing an edge span a 4-cycle, so "every
cycle is a triangle" forces every block to be an edge or a triangle, and conversely.

This file sets up the basic theory:

* `TriangularForest.IsTriangularForest` — the definition;
* closure under subgraphs (`IsTriangularForest.mono`) and induced subgraphs
  (`IsTriangularForest.induce`);
* forests are triangular forests;
* every vertex on a cycle has degree at least two, hence a cycle is no longer than the number
  of vertices of degree at least two (`IsCycle.length_le_card_two_le_degree`);
* consequently any graph with at most three vertices of degree ≥ 2 is a triangular forest
  (`isTriangularForest_of_card_two_le_degree_le_three`), which is the workhorse for verifying
  concrete examples.

open SimpleGraph Finset

variable {V : Type*} {G H : SimpleGraph V}

/-- A graph is a **triangular forest** when every one of its cycles is a triangle. -/
def IsTriangularForest (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∀ ⦃v : V⦄ (c : G.Walk v v), c.IsCycle → c.length = 3

/-- Acyclic graphs (forests) are triangular forests. -/
theorem isTriangularForest_of_isAcyclic (h : G.IsAcyclic) : IsTriangularForest G :=
  fun _ c hc => absurd hc (h c)

/-- The empty graph is a triangular forest. -/
theorem isTriangularForest_bot : IsTriangularForest (⊥ : SimpleGraph V) :=
  isTriangularForest_of_isAcyclic isAcyclic_bot

/-- Triangular forests are closed under taking subgraphs. -/
theorem IsTriangularForest.mono (hle : H ≤ G) (hG : IsTriangularForest G) :
    IsTriangularForest H := by
  intro v c hc
  have := hG (c.mapLe hle) (hc.mapLe hle)
  simpa using this

/-- Triangular forests are closed under taking induced subgraphs. -/
theorem IsTriangularForest.induce (s : Set V) (hG : IsTriangularForest G) :
    IsTriangularForest (G.induce s) := by
  intro v c hc
  have hinj : Function.Injective (SimpleGraph.Embedding.induce (G := G) s).toHom :=

  have := hG (c.map (SimpleGraph.Embedding.induce (G := G) s).toHom) (hc.map hinj)

/-!
# The decision problem: certificates and decidability

The paper *Edge-decomposition into Two Triangular Forests is NP-complete* proves that the
decision problem

> given a graph `G`, can `E(G)` be partitioned into two triangular forests?

is NP-complete.  Membership in NP is the easy half: a decomposition is witnessed by a
**2-colouring of the edges**, an object of size linear in the number of edges, and both colour
classes can be checked to be triangular forests in polynomial time.  This file formalises that
half of the statement structurally:

* `TriangularForest.colorPart` — the colour class of an edge 2-colouring `f : Sym2 V → Bool`;
* `TriangularForest.decomposesIntoTwo_iff_exists_edgeColoring` — a graph decomposes into two
  triangular forests **iff** some edge 2-colouring has both colour classes triangular forests;
  so the search space for a witness is `2^{|E|}` rather than all pairs of graphs;
* `TriangularForest.instDecidableDecomposesIntoTwo` — consequently the decision problem is
  decidable (by a finite search over colourings, each test being decidable by
  `TriangularForest.instDecidableIsTriangularForest`).

Decidability of the *class* `F` and of the *decomposition problem* over `F` are exactly the
hypotheses under which the Lee–Liu–Tsai framework places the problem in NP.
-/

namespace TriangularForest

open SimpleGraph

variable {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V}

/-- The colour class of colour `b` of the edge 2-colouring `f` of `G`. -/
def colorPart (G : SimpleGraph V) (f : Sym2 V → Bool) (b : Bool) : SimpleGraph V :=
  SimpleGraph.fromEdgeSet {e | e ∈ G.edgeSet ∧ f e = b}

@[simp] theorem colorPart_adj {f : Sym2 V → Bool} {b : Bool} {u v : V} :
    (colorPart G f b).Adj u v ↔ G.Adj u v ∧ f s(u, v) = b := by
  simp only [colorPart, fromEdgeSet_adj, Set.mem_setOf_eq, mem_edgeSet]
  exact ⟨fun h => h.1, fun h => ⟨h, h.1.ne⟩⟩

theorem colorPart_le (f : Sym2 V → Bool) (b : Bool) : colorPart G f b ≤ G := by
  intro u v h
  exact (colorPart_adj.1 h).1

/-- The two colour classes of an edge 2-colouring are edge-disjoint. -/
theorem colorPart_disjoint (f : Sym2 V → Bool) :
    Disjoint (colorPart G f true) (colorPart G f false) := by
  rw [disjoint_left]
  intro u v h1 h2
  have e1 := (colorPart_adj.1 h1).2
  have e2 := (colorPart_adj.1 h2).2
  rw [e1] at e2
  exact Bool.noConfusion e2

/-- The two colour classes of an edge 2-colouring cover the graph. -/
theorem colorPart_sup (f : Sym2 V → Bool) :
    colorPart G f true ⊔ colorPart G f false = G := by
  ext u v
  rw [sup_adj, colorPart_adj, colorPart_adj]
  cases f s(u, v) <;> simp

/-- **The decision problem has succinct certificates.**  A graph decomposes into two triangular
forests exactly when its edges can be 2-coloured so that each colour class is a triangular
forest.  This is the NP-membership half of the paper's main theorem: the witness is an edge
colouring (linear in the size of the input) and, by
`TriangularForest.instDecidableIsTriangularForest`, verifying it is an effective test. -/
theorem decomposesIntoTwo_iff_exists_edgeColoring :
    DecomposesIntoTwo G ↔ ∃ f : Sym2 V → Bool,
      IsTriangularForest (colorPart G f true) ∧ IsTriangularForest (colorPart G f false) := by
  classical
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨G₁, G₂, h₁, h₂, hd, hsup⟩
    refine ⟨fun e => decide (e ∈ G₁.edgeSet), ?_, ?_⟩
    · have hEq : colorPart G (fun e => decide (e ∈ G₁.edgeSet)) true = G₁ := by
        ext u v
        rw [colorPart_adj]
        simp only [decide_eq_true_eq, mem_edgeSet]
        refine ⟨fun h => h.2, fun h => ⟨?_, h⟩⟩
        rw [← hsup]
        exact Or.inl h
      rw [hEq]; exact h₁
    · have hEq : colorPart G (fun e => decide (e ∈ G₁.edgeSet)) false = G₂ := by
        ext u v
        rw [colorPart_adj]
        simp only [decide_eq_false_iff_not, mem_edgeSet]
        constructor
        · rintro ⟨hG, hn⟩
          rw [← hsup, sup_adj] at hG
          exact hG.resolve_left hn
        · intro h
          refine ⟨?_, fun hc => disjoint_left.1 hd u v hc h⟩
          rw [← hsup]
          exact Or.inr h
      rw [hEq]; exact h₂
  · rintro ⟨f, h₁, h₂⟩
    exact ⟨colorPart G f true, colorPart G f false, h₁, h₂, colorPart_disjoint f,

decomposition of `G` with a subgraph `H ≤ G` decomposes `H`; hence every obstruction (such as a

theorem DecomposesIntoTwo.mono {H : SimpleGraph V} (h : DecomposesIntoTwo G) (hle : H ≤ G) :
    DecomposesIntoTwo H := by
  obtain ⟨G₁, G₂, h₁, h₂, hd, hsup⟩ := h
  refine ⟨G₁ ⊓ H, G₂ ⊓ H, h₁.mono inf_le_left, h₂.mono inf_le_left,
    hd.mono inf_le_left inf_le_left, ?_⟩
  rw [← inf_sup_right, hsup, inf_eq_right.2 hle]

section Decidable

variable [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]

instance instDecidableRelColorPartAdj (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (f : Sym2 V → Bool) (b : Bool) : DecidableRel (colorPart G f b).Adj := fun _ _ =>
  decidable_of_iff _ colorPart_adj.symm

/-- **The decomposition problem is decidable.**  Combined with
`decomposesIntoTwo_iff_exists_edgeColoring`, the search is over the finitely many edge
2-colourings, and each colour class is tested by the decision procedure for the class. -/
instance instDecidableDecomposesIntoTwo (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] :
    Decidable (DecomposesIntoTwo G) :=
  decidable_of_iff _ decomposesIntoTwo_iff_exists_edgeColoring.symm

end Decidable

/-!
# Sparsity of triangular forests

The main result of this file is that triangular forests are *sparse*: a triangular forest on
`n ≥ 2` vertices has at most `2n - 3` edges (`TriangularForest.card_edgeFinset_add_three_le`).

The proof runs through a longest-path argument, which is the combinatorial heart of the file:

* `TriangularForest.exists_maxPath` — a finite nonempty graph has a path of maximum length;
* `TriangularForest.degree_le_two_of_maxPath_endpoint` — in a triangular forest the endpoint of
  a maximum length path has degree at most two.  Indeed all its neighbours lie on the path (else
  the path could be extended), and a neighbour sitting at distance `ℓ ≥ 2` along the path closes
  a cycle of length `ℓ + 1`, which must be `3`;
* `TriangularForest.exists_degree_le_two` — hence every finite nonempty triangular forest has a
  vertex of degree at most two (triangular forests are `2`-degenerate);
* the edge bound then follows by induction on the number of vertices, deleting a vertex of
  degree at most two.
-/

open SimpleGraph Finset

variable {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V}

/-- If a path from `a` to `x` contains the edge `s(x, a)`, then it is a single edge. -/
theorem length_eq_one_of_mem_edges {a x : V} (q : G.Walk a x) (hq : q.IsPath)
    (h : s(x, a) ∈ q.edges) : q.length = 1 := by
  cases q with
  | nil => simp at h
  | @cons _ c _ hadj q' =>
    rw [Walk.edges_cons, List.mem_cons] at h
    have hq'p : q'.IsPath := hq.of_cons
    rcases h with heq | hmem
    · have hxc : x = c := by
        rw [Sym2.eq_iff] at heq
        rcases heq with ⟨_, ha⟩ | ⟨hx, _⟩
        · exact absurd ha hadj.ne
        · exact hx
      subst hxc
      have hnil : (⟨q', hq'p⟩ : G.Path x x) = SimpleGraph.Path.nil :=
        SimpleGraph.Path.loop_eq _
      have hlen0 : q'.length = 0 := by
        have := congrArg (fun r : G.Path x x => (r : G.Walk x x).length) hnil
        simpa using this
      simp [hlen0]
    · have hain : a ∈ q'.support := Walk.snd_mem_support_of_mem_edges q' hmem
      exact absurd hain ((Walk.cons_isPath_iff hadj q').1 hq).2

/-- A finite nonempty graph has a path of maximum length. -/
theorem exists_maxPath [Fintype V] [Nonempty V] (G : SimpleGraph V) :
    ∃ (a b : V) (p : G.Walk a b), p.IsPath ∧

      ∃ (a b : V) (p : G.Walk a b), p.IsPath ∧ p.length = n} with hS
  obtain ⟨v⟩ := ‹Nonempty V›
  have h0 : 0 ∈ S := by
    simp only [hS, Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_range]
    exact ⟨Fintype.card_pos, v, v, Walk.nil, Walk.IsPath.nil, rfl⟩
  have hne : S.Nonempty := ⟨0, h0⟩
  obtain ⟨a, b, p, hp, hlen⟩ : ∃ (a b : V) (p : G.Walk a b), p.IsPath ∧ p.length = S.max' hne := by
    have := S.max'_mem hne

  refine ⟨a, b, p, hp, fun x y q hq => ?_⟩
  have hq' : q.length ∈ S := by
    simp only [hS, Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_range]
    exact ⟨hq.length_lt, x, y, q, hq, rfl⟩
  rw [hlen]
  exact S.le_max' _ hq'

/-- Every neighbour of the starting point of a maximum length path lies on that path. -/
theorem maxPath_neighbor_mem_support {a b : V} (p : G.Walk a b) (hp : p.IsPath)
    (hmax : ∀ (x y : V) (q : G.Walk x y), q.IsPath → q.length ≤ p.length)
    {x : V} (hx : x ∈ G.neighborFinset a) : x ∈ p.support := by
  by_contra hnot
  have hadj : G.Adj x a := ((G.mem_neighborFinset a x).1 hx).symm
  have hpath : (Walk.cons hadj p).IsPath := hp.cons hnot
  have := hmax x b (Walk.cons hadj p) hpath
  simp [Walk.length_cons] at this

/-- A neighbour of the starting point of a maximum length path in a triangular forest sits at
position `1` or `2` along the path: further along it would close a cycle of length `≥ 4`. -/
theorem maxPath_neighbor_idx {a b : V} (hG : IsTriangularForest G) (p : G.Walk a b)
    (hp : p.IsPath) (hmax : ∀ (x y : V) (q : G.Walk x y), q.IsPath → q.length ≤ p.length)
    {x : V} (hx : x ∈ G.neighborFinset a) :
    p.support.idxOf x = 1 ∨ p.support.idxOf x = 2 := by
  have hxs : x ∈ p.support := maxPath_neighbor_mem_support p hp hmax hx
  have hadj : G.Adj a x := (G.mem_neighborFinset a x).1 hx
  set q := p.takeUntil x hxs with hq
  have hqp : q.IsPath := hp.takeUntil hxs
  have hqlen : q.length = p.support.idxOf x := p.length_takeUntil hxs
  have hne0 : q.length ≠ 0 := by
    intro h0
    have : q.Nil := Walk.nil_iff_length_eq.2 h0
    exact hadj.ne ((p.nil_takeUntil hxs).1 this)
  have hle2 : q.length ≤ 2 := by
    by_contra hgt
    push_neg at hgt
    have hnotedge : s(x, a) ∉ q.edges := fun hmem' => by
      have := length_eq_one_of_mem_edges q hqp hmem'
      omega
    have hcyc : (Walk.cons hadj.symm q).IsCycle :=
      SimpleGraph.Path.cons_isCycle ⟨q, hqp⟩ hadj.symm hnotedge
    have := hG _ hcyc
    rw [Walk.length_cons] at this
    omega
  rw [← hqlen]
  omega

/-- Positions along a path determine vertices, so distinct neighbours of the starting point of a
maximum length path occupy distinct positions. -/
theorem maxPath_idx_injOn {a b : V} (p : G.Walk a b) (hp : p.IsPath)
    (hmax : ∀ (x y : V) (q : G.Walk x y), q.IsPath → q.length ≤ p.length) :
    Set.InjOn (fun x => p.support.idxOf x) (G.neighborFinset a : Set V) := by
  intro x hx y hy hxy
  have hxs : x ∈ p.support := maxPath_neighbor_mem_support p hp hmax (by simpa using hx)
  have hys : y ∈ p.support := maxPath_neighbor_mem_support p hp hmax (by simpa using hy)
  have hx' := p.getVert_support_idxOf hxs
  have hy' := p.getVert_support_idxOf hys
  simp only at hxy
  rw [← hx', ← hy', hxy]

/-- In a triangular forest, the endpoint of a maximum length path has degree at most two. -/
theorem degree_le_two_of_maxPath_endpoint
    (hG : IsTriangularForest G) {a b : V} (p : G.Walk a b) (hp : p.IsPath)
    (hmax : ∀ (x y : V) (q : G.Walk x y), q.IsPath → q.length ≤ p.length) :
    G.degree a ≤ 2 := by
  classical
  have hmaps : Set.MapsTo (fun x => p.support.idxOf x) (G.neighborFinset a : Set V)
      ((({1, 2} : Finset ℕ) : Set ℕ)) := by
    intro x hx
    have := maxPath_neighbor_idx hG p hp hmax (x := x) (by simpa using hx)
    simpa using this
  have := Finset.card_le_card_of_injOn _ hmaps (maxPath_idx_injOn p hp hmax)
  simpa [card_neighborFinset_eq_degree] using this

/-- Every finite nonempty triangular forest has a vertex of degree at most two: triangular

theorem exists_degree_le_two [Fintype V] [Nonempty V] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hG : IsTriangularForest G) : ∃ v : V, G.degree v ≤ 2 := by
  obtain ⟨a, b, p, hp, hmax⟩ := exists_maxPath G
  exact ⟨a, degree_le_two_of_maxPath_endpoint hG p hp hmax⟩

/-- **Sparsity of triangular forests.** A triangular forest on `n ≥ 2` vertices has at most

Triangular forests: numerical demonstrations of the main results.
=================================================================

A *triangular forest* is a graph in which every cycle has length exactly three;
equivalently, every 2-connected block is a single edge or a triangle.

This self-contained script demonstrates, by explicit computation:

  1. Membership testing for the class (block-based, linear time).
  2. The sharp sparsity law   2e <= 3(n-1)   over all graphs on n <= 7 vertices,

  3. Sharpness: the windmill graphs F_k on n = 2k+1 vertices have 3k edges,

     with an explicit K_5 certificate and an exhaustive refutation for K_6.
  5. The clique obstruction: any graph containing a K_6 fails to decompose.
  6. Triangular thickness lower bound  n <= 3k  for covers of K_n, and greedy

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import random
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Edge = FrozenSet[int]
Graph = Tuple[int, FrozenSet[Edge]]  # (number of vertices, edge set)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basic graph utilities
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def edge(u: int, v: int) -> Edge:
    """The undirected edge {u, v}."""
    if u == v:
        raise ValueError("loops are not allowed in a simple graph")
    return frozenset((u, v))


def make_graph(n: int, pairs: Iterable[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Graph:
    """Build a simple graph on vertices 0..n-1 from a list of pairs."""
    return (n, frozenset(edge(u, v) for u, v in pairs))


def complete_graph(n: int) -> Graph:
    """The complete graph K_n."""
    return make_graph(n, itertools.combinations(range(n), 2))


def windmill(k: int) -> Graph:
    """The windmill (friendship) graph F_k: k triangles glued at the hub 0."""
    pairs: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    for i in range(1, k + 1):
        a, b = 2 * i - 1, 2 * i
        pairs += [(0, a), (0, b), (a, b)]
    return make_graph(2 * k + 1, pairs)


def adjacency(g: Graph) -> Dict[int, Set[int]]:
    """Adjacency lists of a graph."""
    n, edges = g
    adj: Dict[int, Set[int]] = {v: set() for v in range(n)}
    for e in edges:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        adj[u].add(v)
        adj[v].add(u)
    return adj


def degrees(g: Graph) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Degree of every vertex."""
    return {v: len(nbrs) for v, nbrs in adjacency(g).items()}


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Membership test for the class of triangular forests
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def triangles_through(g: Graph, e: Edge) -> List[int]:
    """The vertices completing the edge e to a triangle."""
    adj = adjacency(g)
    u, v = tuple(e)
    return sorted(adj[u] & adj[v])


def is_triangular_forest(g: Graph) -> bool:
    """
    Decide whether every cycle of g has length exactly 3.

    Method (Proposition: block description).  Every edge must lie in at most one
    triangle (otherwise two triangles share an edge and span a 4-cycle).  Then
    contract each triangle to a single vertex and test the result for acyclicity:
    the contracted graph is a forest exactly when every block of g was an edge or
    a triangle.
    """
    n, edges = g
    # (i) every edge lies in at most one triangle
    tri_edges: Set[Edge] = set()
    for e in edges:
        common = triangles_through(g, e)
        if len(common) >= 2:
            return False
        if len(common) == 1:
            tri_edges.add(e)

    # (ii) contract the triangles (union-find over triangle edges)
    parent = list(range(n))

    def find(x: int) -> int:
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
            x = parent[x]
        return x

    def union(x: int, y: int) -> None:
        rx, ry = find(x), find(y)
        if rx != ry:
            parent[rx] = ry

    for e in tri_edges:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        union(u, v)

    # (iii) the quotient must be a forest: count components and remaining edges
    remaining = [e for e in edges if e not in tri_edges]
    quotient_edges: Set[Edge] = set()
    for e in remaining:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        ru, rv = find(u), find(v)
        if ru == rv:
            return False  # a non-triangle edge inside a contracted blob
        q = frozenset((ru, rv))
        if q in quotient_edges:
            return False  # parallel edges in the quotient = a longer cycle
        quotient_edges.add(q)

    roots = {find(v) for v in range(n)}
    # forest test: |E| <= |V| - #components, checked via union-find on the quotient
    parent2 = {r: r for r in roots}

    def find2(x: int) -> int:
        while parent2[x] != x:
            parent2[x] = parent2[parent2[x]]
            x = parent2[x]
        return x

    for q in quotient_edges:
        a, b = tuple(q)
        ra, rb = find2(a), find2(b)
        if ra == rb:
            return False  # cycle in the quotient
        parent2[ra] = rb
    return True


def brute_force_is_triangular_forest(g: Graph) -> bool:
    """Reference implementation: enumerate all cycles and check their lengths."""
    n, edges = g
    adj = adjacency(g)
    for length in range(4, n + 1):
        for verts in itertools.permutations(range(n), length):
            if verts[0] != min(verts):
                continue
            if verts[1] > verts[-1]:
                continue  # kill the reflection
            if all(verts[(i + 1) % length] in adj[verts[i]] for i in range(length)):
                return False
    return True


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2-3. The sharp sparsity law and its extremal graphs
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def max_edges_triangular_forest(n: int) -> Tuple[int, Optional[Graph]]:
    """Exhaustively maximise the edge count over triangular forests on n vertices."""
    all_pairs = list(itertools.combinations(range(n), 2))
    best, witness = 0, None
    for size in range(len(all_pairs), -1, -1):
        found = False
        for subset in itertools.combinations(all_pairs, size):
            g = make_graph(n, subset)
            if is_triangular_forest(g):
                best, witness, found = size, g, True
                break
        if found:
            break
    return best, witness


def sparsity_bound(n: int) -> int:
    """The sharp bound floor(3(n-1)/2) on the number of edges."""
    return (3 * (n - 1)) // 2


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Decomposition into two triangular forests
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def decompose_into_two(g: Graph) -> Optional[Tuple[Graph, Graph]]:
    """
    Search for a partition of E(g) into two triangular forests.

    Backtracking over an edge 2-colouring, using the fact that the class is closed
    under subgraphs: a partial colour class that is already not a triangular forest
    can never become one, so the partial test is a sound pruning rule.
    """
    n, edges = g
    # density prescreen: a decomposable graph satisfies |E| <= 3(n-1)
    if n >= 1 and len(edges) > 3 * (n - 1):
        return None
    order = sorted(edges, key=lambda e: sorted(e))
    part: List[List[Edge]] = [[], []]

    def backtrack(i: int) -> bool:
        if i == len(order):
            return True
        for side in (0, 1):
            part[side].append(order[i])
            if is_triangular_forest((n, frozenset(part[side]))) and backtrack(i + 1):
                return True
            part[side].pop()
        return False

    if not backtrack(0):
        return None
    return (n, frozenset(part[0])), (n, frozenset(part[1]))


def contains_k6(g: Graph) -> bool:
    """Does g contain six mutually adjacent vertices?"""
    n, _ = g
    adj = adjacency(g)
    for six in itertools.combinations(range(n), 6):
        if all(b in adj[a] for a, b in itertools.combinations(six, 2)):
            return True
    return False


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Triangular thickness
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def greedy_cover(g: Graph, tries: int = 4000, seed: int = 20260818) -> List[Graph]:
    """
    Randomised search for a cover of E(g) by few triangular forests.

    Repeatedly peel off a maximal triangular forest under a random edge order and
    keep the best (fewest parts) result over `tries` restarts.  Las Vegas: every
    output part is verified to belong to the class.
    """
    n, edges = g
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    best: Optional[List[Graph]] = None
    for _ in range(tries):
        remaining = set(edges)
        parts: List[Graph] = []
        while remaining:
            order = list(remaining)
            rng.shuffle(order)
            chosen: List[Edge] = []
            for e in order:
                if is_triangular_forest((n, frozenset(chosen + [e]))):
                    chosen.append(e)
            parts.append((n, frozenset(chosen)))
            remaining -= set(chosen)
        if best is None or len(parts) < len(best):
            best = parts
        if best is not None and len(best) <= -(-n // 3):
            break
    assert best is not None
    for p in best:
        assert is_triangular_forest(p)
    return best

    """Readable rendering of a graph's edge set."""
    _, edges = g
    return "{" + ", ".join(f"{min(e)}{max(e)}" for e in sorted(edges, key=lambda e: sorted(e))) + "}"

    print("   n | max e over all triangular forests | floor(3(n-1)/2) | 2n-3 (weak bound)")

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Edge = FrozenSet[int]


def adjacency(n: int, edges: Iterable[Edge]) -> Dict[int, Set[int]]:
    adj: Dict[int, Set[int]] = {v: set() for v in range(n)}
    for e in edges:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        adj[u].add(v)
        adj[v].add(u)
    return adj


def is_triangular_forest(n: int, edges: Sequence[Edge]) -> bool:
    """Every cycle has length 3: no edge in two triangles, contraction is a forest."""
    adj = adjacency(n, edges)
    tri: Set[Edge] = set()
    for e in edges:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        common = adj[u] & adj[v]
        if len(common) >= 2:
            return False
        if len(common) == 1:
            tri.add(e)
    parent = list(range(n))

    def find(x: int) -> int:
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
            x = parent[x]
        return x

    for e in tri:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        parent[find(u)] = find(v)
    comp = list(range(n))

    def find2(x: int) -> int:
        while comp[x] != x:
            comp[x] = comp[comp[x]]
            x = comp[x]
        return x

    seen: Set[Edge] = set()
    for e in edges:
        if e in tri:
            continue
        u, v = tuple(e)
        ru, rv = find(u), find(v)
        if ru == rv:
            return False
        q = frozenset((ru, rv))
        if q in seen:
            return False
        seen.add(q)
        a, b = find2(ru), find2(rv)
        if a == b:
            return False
        comp[a] = b
    return True


def decompose_into_two(n: int, edges: Sequence[Edge]) -> Optional[Tuple[List[Edge], List[Edge]]]:
    """Backtracking search over edge 2-colourings, pruned by subgraph closure."""
    if len(edges) > 3 * max(n - 1, 0):
        return None
    order = sorted(edges, key=lambda e: sorted(e))
    part: Tuple[List[Edge], List[Edge]] = ([], [])

    def bt(i: int) -> bool:
        if i == len(order):
            return True
        for side in (0, 1):
            part[side].append(order[i])
            if is_triangular_forest(n, part[side]) and bt(i + 1):
                return True
            part[side].pop()
        return False

    return (part[0], part[1]) if bt(0) else None

    """Least number of edges to delete from K_n before the rest splits into two."""

            res = decompose_into_two(n, keep)

    "recognition": """"Recognition of triangular forests by triangle contraction."""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Set, Tuple

Edge = FrozenSet[int]


class UnionFind:
    """Disjoint-set forest with path halving and union by index."""

    def __init__(self, n: int) -> None:
        self.parent: List[int] = list(range(n))

    def find(self, x: int) -> int:
        while self.parent[x] != x:
            self.parent[x] = self.parent[self.parent[x]]
            x = self.parent[x]
        return x

    def union(self, x: int, y: int) -> bool:
        """Merge the classes of x and y; return False if they were already equal."""
        rx, ry = self.find(x), self.find(y)
        if rx == ry:
            return False
        self.parent[rx] = ry
        return True


def adjacency(n: int, edges: Iterable[Edge]) -> Dict[int, Set[int]]:
    """Adjacency sets of a simple graph on the vertices 0..n-1."""
    adj: Dict[int, Set[int]] = {v: set() for v in range(n)}
    for e in edges:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        adj[u].add(v)
        adj[v].add(u)
    return adj


def is_triangular_forest(n: int, edges: Iterable[Edge]) -> bool:
    """
    Decide whether every cycle of the graph has length exactly three.

    Correctness rests on two facts.  First, in such a graph no edge can lie in two
    triangles: two triangles sharing an edge span a 4-cycle.  Second, once the
    triangles are pairwise edge-disjoint, contracting each of them to a point
    leaves a graph whose cycles correspond exactly to the cycles of length at
    least four of the original; so the contraction must be a forest.
    """
    edges = list(edges)
    adj = adjacency(n, edges)

    triangle_edges: Set[Edge] = set()
    for e in edges:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        common = adj[u] & adj[v]
        if len(common) >= 2:
            return False                       # an edge in two triangles
        if len(common) == 1:
            triangle_edges.add(e)

    blobs = UnionFind(n)
    for e in triangle_edges:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        blobs.union(u, v)

    quotient = UnionFind(n)
    seen: Set[Edge] = set()
    for e in edges:
        if e in triangle_edges:
            continue
        u, v = tuple(e)
        ru, rv = blobs.find(u), blobs.find(v)
        if ru == rv:
            return False                       # a chord inside a contracted blob
        q = frozenset((ru, rv))
        if q in seen:
            return False                       # parallel edges: a long cycle
        seen.add(q)
        if not quotient.union(ru, rv):
            return False                       # a cycle in the contraction
    return True
